\label{th:NIS_Gaussian_src}
	Given parameters $k \ge 2$, $\rho \in (0,1)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an explicitly computable $n_0 = n_0(\rho, k, \varepsilon)$ such that the following holds:
	
	\noindent For any $N$, and any $A : {\mathbb R}^N \to \Delta_k$ and $B : {\mathbb R}^N \to \Delta_k$, there exist functions $\wtilde{A} : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to \Delta_k$ and $\wtilde{B} : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to \Delta_k$ such that,
	\[d_{\mathrm{TV}}\inparen{(A(\mathbf{X}),B(\mathbf{Y}))_{(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}) \sim \mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes N}},\ (\wtilde{A}({\bm a}), \wtilde{B}({\bm b}))_{({\bm a}, {\bm b}) \sim \mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n_0}}} ~\le~ \varepsilon\;.\]
	Moreover, there exists an explicitly computable $d_0 = d_0(\rho, k, \varepsilon)$ for which there are degree-$d_0$ polynomials $A_0 : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B_0 : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to {\mathbb R}^k$, such that, $\wtilde{A}({\bm a}) = \mathcal{R}\inparen{A_0\inparen{\frac{{\bm a}}{\|{\bm a}\|_2}}}$ and $\wtilde{B}({\bm b}) = \mathcal{R}\inparen{B_0\inparen{\frac{{\bm b}}{\|{\bm b}\|_2}}}$.\\
	The explicit $n_0$ and $d_0$ are upper bounded as $n_0 \le \exp \inparen{\mathrm{poly}\inparen{k, \frac{1}{1-\rho}, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}}}$ and $d_0 \le \mathrm{poly}\inparen{k, \frac{1}{1-\rho}, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}}$.\\
	
	\noindent In fact, the transformation satisfies a stronger property that there exists an ``oblivious'' randomized transformation (with a shared random seed) to go from $A$ to $\wtilde{A}$ and from $B$ to $\wtilde{B}$, which works with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$. Since the same transformation is applied on $A$ and $B$ simultaneously with the same random seed, if $A = B$, then the transformation gives $\wtilde{A}=\wtilde{B}$ as well.

\label{thm:decidability}
	Given a joint probability space $(\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu)$ and a family of joint probability spaces $V$ supported over $[k] \times [k]$, and an error parameter $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an algorithm that runs in time $T(\mu, k, \varepsilon)$ (which is an explicitly computable function), and decides $\text{\sc Gap-NIS}((\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu), V, k, \varepsilon)$.
	
	\noindent The run time $T(\mu, k, \varepsilon)$ is upper bounded by $\exp\exp\exp\inparen{\mathrm{poly}\inparen{k, \ \frac{1}{\varepsilon}, \ \frac{1}{1-\rho_0}, \ \log\inparen{\frac{1}{\alpha}}}}$,
	where $\rho_0 = \rho(\mu)$ is the maximal correlation of $(\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu)$ and $\alpha \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} \alpha(\mu)$ is the minimum non-zero probability in $\mu$.

The run time T(mu, k, varepsilon) is upper bounded by expexpexpinparenpolyinparenk, \ frac1varepsilon, \ frac11-rho_0, \ loginparenfrac1alpha, where rho_0 = rho(mu) is the maximal correlation of (Z times Z, mu) and alpha stackreldef= alpha(mu) is the minimum non-zero probability in mu.

\label{thm:dim-reduction}
	Given parameters $d \in {\mathbb Z}_{> 0}$, $\rho \in [0,1]$ and $\delta > 0$, there exists an \emph{explicitly computable} $D = D(d, \delta)$, such that the following holds:
	
	Let $A: {\mathbb R}^N \to {\mathbb R}$ and $B: {\mathbb R}^N \to {\mathbb R}$ be degree-$d$ multilinear polynomials, such that $\norm{2}{A}, \norm{2}{B} \le 1$.\\
	For column vectors ${\bm a}, {\bm b} \in {\mathbb R}^D$ and $M \in {\mathbb R}^{N \times D}$, define the functions $A_M : {\mathbb R}^D \to {\mathbb R}$ and $B_M : {\mathbb R}^D \to {\mathbb R}$ as
	\[A_M({\bm a}) ~=~ A\inparen{\frac{M {\bm a}}{\norm{2}{{\bm a}}}} \qquad \ \mathrm{and} \ \qquad B_M({\bm b}) = B\inparen{\frac{M {\bm b}}{\norm{2}{{\bm b}}}}\]
	
	\noindent Sample $M \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)^{\otimes (N \times D)}$. Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the choice of $M$, it holds that,
	\[\inabs{\inangle{A_M, B_M}_{\mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes D}} ~-~ \inangle{A, B}_{\mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes N}}} ~<~ \delta\;.\]
	In particular, one may take $D = \frac{d^{O(d)}}{\delta^4}$.\\
	
	\noindent In other words, for a typical choice of $M \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)^{\otimes (N \times D)}$, the correlation between $A$ and $B$ is approximately preserved if we replace $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}) \sim \mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes N}$ by $(M {\bm a}/\norm{2}{{\bm a}}, M {\bm b}/\norm{2}{{\bm b}})$, where $({\bm a}, {\bm b}) \sim \mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes D}$. Intuitively, $M$ can be thought of as a means to ``stretch'' $D$ coordinates of $\mathcal{G}_{\rho}$ into effectively $N$ coordinates of $\mathcal{G}_{\rho}$, while ``fooling'' correlations between degree-$d$ multilinear polynomials.

nodes.statement: We invoke Creflem:mean_var_bound with parameters d and delta^2/2, and we get a choice of D = fracd^O(d)delta^4. Using Chebyshev's inequality and using the Variance bound in Creflem:mean_var_bound, we have that for any eta > 0, \[ Pr_M insquareinabsF(M) - E_M F(M) > eta ~le~ fracdelta^22eta\;.\] Using the triangle inequality, and the Mean bound in Creflem:mean_var_bound, we get &Pr_M insquareinabsF(M) - inangleA, B_G_rho^otimes N > delta\\ & ~le~ Pr_M insquareinabsF(M) - E_M F(M) + inabsE_M F(M) - inangleA, B_G_rho^otimes N > delta\\ & ~le~ Pr_M insquareinabsF(M) - E_M F(M) > delta - delta^2\\ & ~le~ delta.qedhere

We invoke \Cref{lem:mean_var_bound} with parameters $d$ and $\delta^2/2$, and we get a choice of $D = \frac{d^{O(d)}}{\delta^4}$. Using Chebyshev's inequality and using the Variance bound in \Cref{lem:mean_var_bound}, we have that for any $\eta > 0$,
	\[ \Pr_M \insquare{\inabs{F(M) - \mathbb{E}_M F(M)} > \eta} ~\le~ \frac{\delta^2}{2\eta}\;.\]
	Using the triangle inequality, and the Mean bound in \Cref{lem:mean_var_bound}, we get
	\begin{align*}
		&\Pr_M \insquare{\inabs{F(M) - \inangle{A, B}_{\mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes N}}} > \delta}\\
		& ~\le~ \Pr_M \insquare{\inabs{F(M) - \mathbb{E}_M F(M)} + \inabs{\mathbb{E}_M F(M) - \inangle{A, B}_{\mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes N}}} > \delta}\\
		& ~\le~ \Pr_M \insquare{\inabs{F(M) - \mathbb{E}_M F(M)} > \delta - \delta^2}\\
		& ~\le~ \delta.\qedhere
	\end{align*}

\label{lem:multilin_main}
	Let $\rho \in [0,1]$, $\delta > 0$, $d, k \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}$ be any given constant parameters. There exists an explicit $t = t(k, d, \delta)$ such that the following holds:\\
	
	\noindent Let $A : {\mathbb R}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B : {\mathbb R}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ be degree-$d$ polynomials, such that, for any $j \in [k]$ : $\mathsf{Var}(A_j), \mathsf{Var}(B_j) \le 1$. Then, there exist functions $A^{(1)} : {\mathbb R}^{nt} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B^{(1)} : {\mathbb R}^{nt} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ such that the following hold
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $A^{(1)}$ and $B^{(1)}$ are multilinear with degree $d$.
		\item For any $j \in [k]$, it holds that $\mathsf{Var}(A^{(1)}_j) \le \mathsf{Var}(A_j) \le 1$ and $\mathsf{Var}(B^{(1)}_j) \le \mathsf{Var}(B_j) \le 1$.
		\item $\norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(A^{(1)}) - A^{(1)}} ~\le~ \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(A) - A} + \delta$ and $\norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(B^{(1)}) - B^{(1)}} ~\le~ \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(B) - B} + \delta$
		\item For any $\ell \in [nt]$ and $j \in [k]$, it holds that $\mathrm{Inf}_\ell(A^{(1)}_j) \le \delta$ and $\mathrm{Inf}_\ell(B^{(1)}_j) \le \delta$.
		\item For every $i, j \in [k]$,
		\[ \inabs{\inangle{A^{(1)}_i, B^{(1)}_j}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes nt}} - \inangle{A_i, B_j}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n}}} ~\le~ \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{k}} \]
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\noindent In particular, one may take $t = O\inparen{\frac{k^2 d^2}{\delta^2}}$.

\label{thm:gaussian-non-int-sim}
	Given parameters $k \ge 2$, $\rho \in [0,1]$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an explicitly computable $n_0 = n_0(\rho, k, \varepsilon)$ such that the following holds:

	\noindent For any $N$, and any $A : {\mathbb R}^N \to \Delta_k$ and $B : {\mathbb R}^N \to \Delta_k$, there exist functions $\wtilde{A} : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to \Delta_k$ and $\wtilde{B} : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to \Delta_k$ such that,
	\[d_{\mathrm{TV}}\inparen{(A(\mathbf{X}),B(\mathbf{Y}))_{(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})\sim \mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes N}},\ (\wtilde{A}({\bm a}), \wtilde{B}({\bm b}))_{({\bm a}, {\bm b}) \sim \mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n_0}}} \le \varepsilon\;.\]
	Moreover, there exists $d_0 = d_0(\rho, k, \varepsilon)$ for which there are degree-$d_0$ polynomials $A_0 : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B_0 : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to {\mathbb R}^k$, such that, $\wtilde{A}({\bm a}) = \mathcal{R}\inparen{A_0\inparen{\frac{{\bm a}}{\|{\bm a}\|_2}}}$ and $\wtilde{B}({\bm b}) = \mathcal{R}\inparen{B_0\inparen{\frac{{\bm b}}{\|{\bm b}\|_2}}}$.\\
	In particular, one may take $n_0 = \exp \inparen{\mathrm{poly}\inparen{k, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}, \frac{1}{1-\rho}}}$ and $d_0 = \mathrm{poly}\inparen{k, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}, \frac{1}{1-\rho}}$.\footnote{the details of the exact value of $n_0$ could be inferred from combining the bounds across various lemmas used. We skip it for brevity, and instead stress on the qualitative nature of the bound.}\\
	
	\noindent In fact, the transformation satisfies a stronger property that there exists an ``oblivious'' randomized transformation (with a shared random seed) to go from $A$ to $\wtilde{A}$ and from $B$ to $\wtilde{B}$, which works with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$. Since the same transformation is applied on $A$ and $B$ simultaneously with the same random seed, if $A = B$, then the transformation gives $\wtilde{A}=\wtilde{B}$ as well.

nodes.statement: For any i, j in [k], we focus on the quantity inangleA_i, B_j_G_rho^otimes n which is the probability of the event that [Alice outputs i and Bob outputs j]. Through several steps, we modify Alice's and Bob's strategies, while approximately preserving this quantity for every i, j. Note that if we preserve the probability that Alice outputs i and Bob outputs j for every i, j upto an additive varepsilon/k^2, this implies that we would preserve the joint distribution of Alice and Bob's outputs up to ell_1-distance of varepsilon. \label{thm:non-int-sim}
	Let $(\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu)$ be a joint probability space. Given parameters $k \ge 2$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an explicitly computable $n_0 = n_0(\mu, k, \varepsilon)$ such that the following holds:
	
	Let $A : \mathcal{Z}^N \to \Delta_k$ and $B : \mathcal{Z}^N \to \Delta_k$. Then there exist functions $\wtilde{A} : \mathcal{Z}^{n_0} \to \Delta_k$ and $\wtilde{B} : \mathcal{Z}^{n_0} \to \Delta_k$ such that,
	\[d_{\mathrm{TV}}\inparen{(A({\bm x}),B({\bm y}))_{({\bm x},{\bm y})\sim \mu^{\otimes N}}, \ (\wtilde{A}({\bm a}), \wtilde{B}({\bm b}))_{{\bm a}, {\bm b} \sim \mu^{\otimes n_0}}} \le \varepsilon\;.\]
	In particular, $n_0$ is an explicit function upper bounded by $\exp\inparen{\mathrm{poly}\inparen{k, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}, \frac{1}{1-\rho}, \log\inparen{\frac{1}{\alpha}}}}$\footnote{the details of the exact value of $n_0$ could be inferred from combining the bounds across various lemmas used. We skip it for brevity, and instead stress on the qualitative nature of the bound.}, where $\alpha = \alpha(\mu)$ is the smallest atom in $\mu$ and $\rho = \rho(\mu)$ is the maximal correlation of $\mu$.

nodes.name: \bf Proof Overview
nodes.statement: : The proof works by a reduction to Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim. This reduction is done along the same framework as introduced in . We first apply a Smoothing operation (Creflem:smoothing_main) similar to the Gaussian case, to make the functions A and B have low-degree. Next, we will apply a Regularity Lemma (Creflem:joint_regularity), to identify a constant sized subset of coordinates, such that for a random fixing of these coordinates, the restricted function is low influential on the remaining coordinates. This allows us to apply the invariance principle (Creflem:our_invariance) to replace the coordinates of Alice and Bob on the remaining coordinates by rho-correlated Gaussians. We now use Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim to reduce the number of coordinates of rho-correlated Gaussians needed. Finally, we wish to get the strategies to use samples from mu instead of G_rho, by simulating the correlated multivariate Gaussians using a bounded number of samples of mu. However, after the transformation of Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim, the resulting function might be none of low-degree, multilinear or low-influential. To get around this we apply Smoothing (Creflem:smoothing_main) to make it low-degree and Multilinearization (Creflem:multilin_main) to make it multilinear and low-influential, after which we can apply the invariance principle (Creflem:our_invariance). An overview of the transformations done is presented in Creffig:General_NIS.
nodes.raw_latex: : The proof works by a reduction to \Cref{thm:gaussian-non-int-sim}. This reduction is done along the same framework as introduced in \cite{GKS_NIS_decidable}. We first apply a Smoothing operation (\Cref{lem:smoothing_main}) similar to the Gaussian case, to make the functions $A$ and $B$ have {\em low-degree}. Next, we will apply a Regularity Lemma (\Cref{lem:joint_regularity}), to identify a constant sized subset of coordinates, such that for a random fixing of these coordinates, the restricted function is low influential on the remaining coordinates. This allows us to apply the invariance principle (\Cref{lem:our_invariance}) to replace the coordinates of Alice and Bob on the remaining coordinates by $\rho$-correlated Gaussians. We now use \Cref{thm:gaussian-non-int-sim} to reduce the number of coordinates of $\rho$-correlated Gaussians needed. Finally, we wish to get the strategies to use samples from $\mu$ instead of $\mathcal{G}_{\rho}$, by simulating the correlated multivariate Gaussians using a bounded number of samples of $\mu$. However, after the transformation of \Cref{thm:gaussian-non-int-sim}, the resulting function might be none of low-degree, multilinear or low-influential. To get around this we apply Smoothing (\Cref{lem:smoothing_main}) to make it low-degree and Multilinearization (\Cref{lem:multilin_main}) to make it multilinear and low-influential, after which we can apply the invariance principle (\Cref{lem:our_invariance}). An overview of the transformations done is presented in \Cref{fig:General_NIS}.
nodes.clean_text: : The proof works by a reduction to Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim. This reduction is done along the same framework as introduced in . We first apply a Smoothing operation (Creflem:smoothing_main) similar to the Gaussian case, to make the functions A and B have low-degree. Next, we will apply a Regularity Lemma (Creflem:joint_regularity), to identify a constant sized subset of coordinates, such that for a random fixing of these coordinates, the restricted function is low influential on the remaining coordinates. This allows us to apply the invariance principle (Creflem:our_invariance) to replace the coordinates of Alice and Bob on the remaining coordinates by rho-correlated Gaussians. We now use Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim to reduce the number of coordinates of rho-correlated Gaussians needed. Finally, we wish to get the strategies to use samples from mu instead of G_rho, by simulating the correlated multivariate Gaussians using a bounded number of samples of mu. However, after the transformation of Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim, the resulting function might be none of low-degree, multilinear or low-influential. To get around this we apply Smoothing (Creflem:smoothing_main) to make it low-degree and Multilinearization (Creflem:multilin_main) to make it multilinear and low-influential, after which we can apply the invariance principle (Creflem:our_invariance). An overview of the transformations done is presented in Creffig:General_NIS.

nodes.statement: Crefthm:non-int-sim As in the proof of Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim, for any i, j in [k], we focus on the quantity inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes n which is the probability of the event that [Alice outputs i and Bob outputs j]. Through the several steps we modify Alice's and Bob's strategy, while preserving this quantity approximately for every i, j. If we preserve the probability that Alice outputs i and Bob outputs j for every i, j upto an additive varepsilon/k^2, it implies that we preserve the joint distribution of Alice and Bob's outputs up to an ell_1-distance of varepsilon. captionDependency of parameters in the proof of Crefthm:non-int-sim paragraphChoice of parameters \& bound on n_0. As described in the overview, we are going to invoke several of the lemmas we have developed in our proof. We now describe the choice of parameters for which we invoke these lemmas, thereby obtaining our final explicit bound on n_0. We recommend consulting Creffig:dependency to follow the exact chain of dependencies among the parameters (the dependencies on mu and k are suppressed in the figure for clarity). Let delta be a running parameter, that we finalize at the end (in terms of mu, k and varepsilon). We wish to invoke the Smoothing operation over Z^N (Creflem:smoothing_main) with parameter delta. This dictates a value of d = d(rho, k, delta), which is the degree of the polynomials obtained after smoothing. We will invoke the Invariance Principle (Creflem:our_invariance) with parameters delta and d as obtained just now. This dictates a value of tau = tau(mu, k, d, delta), which is the bound on the influence needed in order to apply the invariance principle. We will invoke the Regularity Lemma (Creflem:joint_regularity) with parameters d and tau as obtained above. This dictates a value of h = h(mu,k,d,tau), which is the bound on number of head coordinates that need to be fixed to get all influences less than tau on the remaining coordinates, for a random restriction of the head coordinates. We will apply Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim with the error parameter varepsilon as delta. This dictates a value of D = n_0(k,rho,delta), which the number of coordinates of correlated Gaussians needed after dimension reduction. In order to go back from correlated Gaussians to samples from (Z times Z; mu), we will again apply the Smoothing operation, this time over Gaussian space (Creflem:smoothing_main) with parameter delta, which again dictates a value of d = d(rho, k, delta). We will again apply the Invariance principle (Creflem:our_invariance) with parameters delta and d as obtained just now. This dictates a value of tau = tau(mu, k, d, delta), which is the bound on the influence needed in order to apply the invariance principle. In order to make the influences small, we will apply the Multilinearization operation (Creflem:multilin_main) with parameters delta gets tau and d as obtained above. This dictates a value of t = t(k,d,delta), which is the blow up incurred while making the polynomials multilinear and to make them have all influences smaller than delta. Finally n_0 = h + D cdot t. Recall that h is the number of head coordinates in the Regularity Lemma. D is the number of coordinates obtained after applying Gaussian NIS (Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim). Finally t is the blow up incurred while going back from correlated Gaussian space to (Z times Z; mu). We will eventually choose delta = varepsilon^2/k^4. It can be inferred by going through all the parameters carefully that n_0(mu, k, varepsilon) is an explicit function that can be upper bounded as exp inparenpoly inparenk, frac1varepsilon, frac11-rho, log inparenfrac1alpha. We skip this the details of this calculation for brevity. paragraphAnalysis of the transformations. We now turn to the analysis of the above transformation. We wish to show that inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes N approx inanglewtildeA_i, wtildeB_j_G_rho^otimes n_0 for every i, j in [k]. We transform A and B through each of the following steps, as illustrated in Creffig:General_NIS. At each step, we approximately preserve the correlation inangleA_i, B_j for every i, j in [k]. draw[-latex] (A7) -- (0 - 3*0.3,-16); draw[-latex] (B7) -- (5+2*0.3,-16); captionTransformations for Non-interactive simulation from Arbitrary Discrete Sources item Smoothing (over hypercube): We apply Creflem:smoothing_main on A and B to get the low-degree versions A^(1) : Z^N to mathbb R^k and B^(1) : Z^N to mathbb R^k. This guarantees that A^(1) and B^(1) have degree at most d. Moreover, we have that for every i, j in [k], \[ inabsinangleA^(1)_i, B^(1)_j_mu^otimes N - inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes N le delta \] Additionally, \[ norm2R(A^(1)) - A^(1) ~le~ norm2R(A) - A + delta ~le~ delta\;.\] Similarly, we also have that, \[norm2R(B^(1)) - B^(1) ~le~ delta\] Using Creflem:close-strategies, we can conclude that for every i, j in [k], inabsinangleR_i(A^(1)), R_j(B^(1))_mu^otimes N - inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes N ~le~ 3delta item Regularity Lemma: We apply Creflem:joint_regularity to identify a subset H subseteq [n] with |H| = h, such that, for a random restriction (bm x_H, bm y_H) sim mu^otimes h, it holds with probability at least 1-tau, that the restricted functions (A^(1)_i)^bm x_H : Z^N-h to mathbb R^k and (B^(1)_i)^bm y_H : Z^N-h to mathbb R^k have all individual influences smaller than tau, for any i in [k]. We call a restriction (bm x_H, bm y_H) as ``good'' in this case, and ``bad'' otherwise. Note that any such restriction (``good'' or ``bad'') has degree at most d. For the rest of the steps, we will focus on a good (bm x_H, bm y_H). For convenience, define N_1 = N-h. item Invariance Principle (from Z to mathbb R): For a good (bm x_H, bm y_H), we apply Creflem:our_invariance on (A^(1))^bm x_H and (B^(1))^bm y_H to get functions (A^(2))^bm x_H : mathbb R^N_2 to Delta_k and (B^(2))^bm y_H : mathbb R^N_2 to Delta_k (where N_2 = N_1 cdot (q-1)), such that for every i, j in [k], inabsinangle(A^(2)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(2)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes N_2 - inangleR_iinparen(A^(1))^bm x_H, R_jinparen(B^(1))^bm y_H_mu^otimes N_1 ~le~ delta Note that strictly speaking Creflem:our_invariance, as stated, gives us functions mapping to mathbb R^k and not Delta_k. However, we consider their rounded versions, which exactly gives us the statement above. item Dimension Reduction: We apply Crefthm:dim-reduction on (A^(2))^bm x_H and (B^(2))^bm y_H, to get functions (A^(3))^bm x_H : mathbb R^D to Delta_k and (B^(3))^bm y_H : mathbb R^D to Delta_k, such that, for every i, j in [k], inabsinangle(A^(3)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(3)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D - inangle(A^(2)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(2)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes N_2 ~le~ delta Note that this is the only randomized step in the entire transformation. This reduction succeeds with probability at least 1 - 4delta for every good (bm x_H, bm y_H). For a fixed choice of the random seed, we call a good (bm x_H, bm y_H) as ``lucky''footnoterather poor choice of terminology, given that most (bm x_H, bm y_H) end up being lucky! if the reduction succeeds for that (bm x_H, bm y_H). In expectation over the choice of random seeds, a (1-4delta) fraction of the good (bm x_H, bm y_H) are going to be lucky. We can hence choose a choice of random seed for which indeed a (1-4delta) fraction of the good (bm x_H, bm y_H) are lucky. On the other hand, Regularity Lemma ensures that with probability 1-delta, a sampled (bm x_H, bm y_H) will be good. This gives that for the said choice of random seed in Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim, with probability at least 1-5delta, the sampled (bm x_H, bm y_H) is both good and lucky. For the rest of the steps, we will focus on a good and lucky (bm x_H, bm y_H). item Smoothing (over Gaussian space): We again apply Creflem:smoothing_main on (A^(3))^bm x_H and (B^(3))^bm y_H to get the low-degree versions (A^(4))^bm x_H : mathbb R^D to mathbb R^k and (B^(4))^bm y_H : mathbb R^D to mathbb R^k. This guarantees that (A^(4))^bm x_H and (B^(4))^bm y_H have degree at most d. Moreover, we have that for every i, j in [k], inabsinangle(A^(4)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(4)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D - inangle(A^(3)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(3)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D ~le~ delta Additionally, \[ norm2R(A^(4)) - A^(4) ~le~ delta \ and \ norm2R(B^(4)) - B^(4) ~le~ delta \] item Multilinearization: We apply Creflem:multilin_main on (A^(4))^bm x_H and (B^(4))^bm y_H to get the multilinearized and low-influential versions (A^(5))^bm x_H : mathbb R^D_1 to mathbb R^k and (B^(5))^bm y_H : mathbb R^D_1 to mathbb R^k (where D_1 = Dt). Thus, we have for every i, j in [k], \[ inabsinangle(A^(5)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(5)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D_1 - inangle(A^(4)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(4)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D ~le~ delta \] Additionally, combining with Creflem:close-to-simplex, \[ norm2R(A^(5)) - A^(5) ~le~ norm2R(A^(4)) - A^(4) + norm2A^(5) - A^(4) ~le~ 2delta \] Similarly, \[ norm2R(B^(5)) - B^(5) ~le~ 2delta \] Combining all this with Creflem:close-strategies we get that, inabsinangleR_iinparen(A^(5))^bm x_H, R_jinparen(B^(5))^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D_1 - inangle(A^(4)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(4)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D ~le~ 5delta Additionally, note that we also have that Inf_ell((A^(5)_i))^bm x_H le tau and Inf_ell((B^(5)_i))^bm y_H le tau for all i in [k] and ell in [n]. This is helpful for us to apply the invariance principle next. item Invariance Principle (from mathbb R to Z): We apply Creflem:our_invariance on (A^(5))^bm x_H and (B^(5))^bm y_H to get functions (A^(6))^bm x_H : Z^D_1 to Delta_k and (B^(6))^bm y_H : Z^D_1 to Delta_k, such that for every i, j in [k], inabsinangle(A^(6)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(6)_j)^bm y_H_mu^otimes D_1 - inangleR_iinparen(A^(5))^bm x_H, R_jinparen(B^(5))^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D_1 ~le~ delta Note again that strictly speaking Creflem:our_invariance gives us functions mapping to mathbb R^k and not Delta_k. However, we consider their rounded versions, which exactly gives us the statement above. paragraphPutting it together. We now show how to put together Crefeqn:NIS-1,eqn:NIS-2,eqn:NIS-3,eqn:NIS-4,eqn:NIS-5,eqn:NIS-6 to get our final conclusion. We now define our final functions wtildeA : Z^n_0 to Delta_k and wtildeB : Z^n_0 to Delta_k as follows. Firstly, we interpret the n_0 = h + D_1 coordinates of bm x as two parts: head coordinates bm x_H in Z^h and the remaining coordinates bm x_R in Z^D_1. Similarly for bm y. \[ wtildeA(bm x) = wtildeA(bm x_H, bm x_R) = (A^(6))^bm x_H(bm x_R) \ and \ wtildeB(bm y) = wtildeB(bm y_H, bm y_R) = (B^(6))^bm y_H(bm y_R)\;.\] We now show that for all i, j in [k], it holds that, \[ inabsinanglewtildeA_i, wtildeB_j_mu^otimes n_0 - inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes N ~le~ O(delta) \] We note that, & inanglewtildeA_i, wtildeB_j_mu^otimes n_0 \\ &~=~ E_(bm x_H, bm y_H) sim mu^otimes h inangle(A^(6)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(6)_j)^bm y_H_mu^otimes D_1\\ &~=~ Prinbmat(bm x_H, bm y_H) is \\ (good and em lucky) cdot E_substack(bm x_H, bm y_H) sim mu^otimes h\\ | \ good \& em lucky inangle(A^(6)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(6)_j)^bm y_H_mu^otimes D_1\\ & ~+~ Prinbmat(bm x_H, bm y_H) is not \\ (good and em lucky) cdot E_substack(bm x_H, bm y_H) sim mu^otimes h\\ | \ not (good \& em lucky) inangle(A^(6)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(6)_j)^bm y_H_mu^otimes D_1\\ &~=~ Prinbmat(bm x_H, bm y_H) is \\ (good and em lucky) cdot E_substack(bm x_H, bm y_H) sim mu^otimes h\\ | \ good \& em lucky inangle(A^(6)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(6)_j)^bm y_H_mu^otimes D_1 ~pm~ O(delta)\\ & ldots inparensince Prinbmat(bm x_H, bm y_H) is not \\ (good and em lucky) le O(delta)\\ &~=~ Prinbmat(bm x_H, bm y_H) is \\ (good and em lucky) cdot E_substack(bm x_H, bm y_H) sim mu^otimes h\\ | \ good \& em lucky inangleR_iinparen(A^(1))^bm x_H, R_jinparen(B^(1))^bm y_H_mu^otimes N_1 ~pm~ O(delta)\\ & ldots inpareninmatcombining Crefeqn:NIS-2,eqn:NIS-3,eqn:NIS-4,eqn:NIS-5,eqn:NIS-6\\ which hold for good and em lucky (bm x_H,bm y_H)\\ &~=~ E_(bm x_H, bm y_H) sim mu^otimes h inangleR_iinparen(A^(1))^bm x_H, R_jinparen(B^(1))^bm y_H_mu^otimes N_1 ~pm~ O(delta)\\ & ldots inparensince Prinbmat(bm x_H, bm y_H) is \\ (good and em lucky) in [1-O(delta), \ 1]\\ &~=~ inangleR_i(A^(1)), R_j(B^(1))_mu^otimes N ~pm~ O(delta)\\ &~=~ inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes N ~pm~ O(delta) ldots(using Crefeqn:NIS-1) Thus, more strongly, if we instantiate delta as O(varepsilon/k^2), then we get that \[d_TVinparen(A(bm x),B(bm y))_(bm x,bm y)sim mu^otimes N, \ (wtildeA(bm a), wtildeB(bm b))_bm a, bm b sim mu^otimes n_0 le varepsilon\;.\]

captionDependency of parameters in the proof of Crefthm:non-int-sim paragraphChoice of parameters \& bound on n_0. As described in the overview, we are going to invoke several of the lemmas we have developed in our proof. We now describe the choice of parameters for which we invoke these lemmas, thereby obtaining our final explicit bound on n_0. We recommend consulting Creffig:dependency to follow the exact chain of dependencies among the parameters (the dependencies on mu and k are suppressed in the figure for clarity). Let delta be a running parameter, that we finalize at the end (in terms of mu, k and varepsilon). We wish to invoke the Smoothing operation over Z^N (Creflem:smoothing_main) with parameter delta. This dictates a value of d = d(rho, k, delta), which is the degree of the polynomials obtained after smoothing. We will invoke the Invariance Principle (Creflem:our_invariance) with parameters delta and d as obtained just now. This dictates a value of tau = tau(mu, k, d, delta), which is the bound on the influence needed in order to apply the invariance principle. We will invoke the Regularity Lemma (Creflem:joint_regularity) with parameters d and tau as obtained above. This dictates a value of h = h(mu,k,d,tau), which is the bound on number of head coordinates that need to be fixed to get all influences less than tau on the remaining coordinates, for a random restriction of the head coordinates. We will apply Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim with the error parameter varepsilon as delta. This dictates a value of D = n_0(k,rho,delta), which the number of coordinates of correlated Gaussians needed after dimension reduction. In order to go back from correlated Gaussians to samples from (Z times Z; mu), we will again apply the Smoothing operation, this time over Gaussian space (Creflem:smoothing_main) with parameter delta, which again dictates a value of d = d(rho, k, delta). We will again apply the Invariance principle (Creflem:our_invariance) with parameters delta and d as obtained just now. This dictates a value of tau = tau(mu, k, d, delta), which is the bound on the influence needed in order to apply the invariance principle. In order to make the influences small, we will apply the Multilinearization operation (Creflem:multilin_main) with parameters delta gets tau and d as obtained above. This dictates a value of t = t(k,d,delta), which is the blow up incurred while making the polynomials multilinear and to make them have all influences smaller than delta. Finally n_0 = h + D cdot t. Recall that h is the number of head coordinates in the Regularity Lemma. D is the number of coordinates obtained after applying Gaussian NIS (Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim). Finally t is the blow up incurred while going back from correlated Gaussian space to (Z times Z; mu). We will eventually choose delta = varepsilon^2/k^4. It can be inferred by going through all the parameters carefully that n_0(mu, k, varepsilon) is an explicit function that can be upper bounded as exp inparenpoly inparenk, frac1varepsilon, frac11-rho, log inparenfrac1alpha. We skip this the details of this calculation for brevity. paragraphAnalysis of the transformations. We now turn to the analysis of the above transformation. We wish to show that inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes N approx inanglewtildeA_i, wtildeB_j_G_rho^otimes n_0 for every i, j in [k]. We transform A and B through each of the following steps, as illustrated in Creffig:General_NIS. At each step, we approximately preserve the correlation inangleA_i, B_j for every i, j in [k]. draw[-latex] (A7) -- (0 - 3*0.3,-16); draw[-latex] (B7) -- (5+2*0.3,-16); captionTransformations for Non-interactive simulation from Arbitrary Discrete Sources item Smoothing (over hypercube): We apply Creflem:smoothing_main on A and B to get the low-degree versions A^(1) : Z^N to mathbb R^k and B^(1) : Z^N to mathbb R^k. This guarantees that A^(1) and B^(1) have degree at most d. Moreover, we have that for every i, j in [k], \[ inabsinangleA^(1)_i, B^(1)_j_mu^otimes N - inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes N le delta \] Additionally, \[ norm2R(A^(1)) - A^(1) ~le~ norm2R(A) - A + delta ~le~ delta\;.\] Similarly, we also have that, \[norm2R(B^(1)) - B^(1) ~le~ delta\] Using Creflem:close-strategies, we can conclude that for every i, j in [k], inabsinangleR_i(A^(1)), R_j(B^(1))_mu^otimes N - inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes N ~le~ 3delta item Regularity Lemma: We apply Creflem:joint_regularity to identify a subset H subseteq [n] with |H| = h, such that, for a random restriction (bm x_H, bm y_H) sim mu^otimes h, it holds with probability at least 1-tau, that the restricted functions (A^(1)_i)^bm x_H : Z^N-h to mathbb R^k and (B^(1)_i)^bm y_H : Z^N-h to mathbb R^k have all individual influences smaller than tau, for any i in [k]. We call a restriction (bm x_H, bm y_H) as ``good'' in this case, and ``bad'' otherwise. Note that any such restriction (``good'' or ``bad'') has degree at most d. For the rest of the steps, we will focus on a good (bm x_H, bm y_H). For convenience, define N_1 = N-h. item Invariance Principle (from Z to mathbb R): For a good (bm x_H, bm y_H), we apply Creflem:our_invariance on (A^(1))^bm x_H and (B^(1))^bm y_H to get functions (A^(2))^bm x_H : mathbb R^N_2 to Delta_k and (B^(2))^bm y_H : mathbb R^N_2 to Delta_k (where N_2 = N_1 cdot (q-1)), such that for every i, j in [k], inabsinangle(A^(2)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(2)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes N_2 - inangleR_iinparen(A^(1))^bm x_H, R_jinparen(B^(1))^bm y_H_mu^otimes N_1 ~le~ delta Note that strictly speaking Creflem:our_invariance, as stated, gives us functions mapping to mathbb R^k and not Delta_k. However, we consider their rounded versions, which exactly gives us the statement above. item Dimension Reduction: We apply Crefthm:dim-reduction on (A^(2))^bm x_H and (B^(2))^bm y_H, to get functions (A^(3))^bm x_H : mathbb R^D to Delta_k and (B^(3))^bm y_H : mathbb R^D to Delta_k, such that, for every i, j in [k], inabsinangle(A^(3)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(3)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D - inangle(A^(2)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(2)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes N_2 ~le~ delta Note that this is the only randomized step in the entire transformation. This reduction succeeds with probability at least 1 - 4delta for every good (bm x_H, bm y_H). For a fixed choice of the random seed, we call a good (bm x_H, bm y_H) as ``lucky''footnoterather poor choice of terminology, given that most (bm x_H, bm y_H) end up being lucky! if the reduction succeeds for that (bm x_H, bm y_H). In expectation over the choice of random seeds, a (1-4delta) fraction of the good (bm x_H, bm y_H) are going to be lucky. We can hence choose a choice of random seed for which indeed a (1-4delta) fraction of the good (bm x_H, bm y_H) are lucky. On the other hand, Regularity Lemma ensures that with probability 1-delta, a sampled (bm x_H, bm y_H) will be good. This gives that for the said choice of random seed in Crefthm:gaussian-non-int-sim, with probability at least 1-5delta, the sampled (bm x_H, bm y_H) is both good and lucky. For the rest of the steps, we will focus on a good and lucky (bm x_H, bm y_H). item Smoothing (over Gaussian space): We again apply Creflem:smoothing_main on (A^(3))^bm x_H and (B^(3))^bm y_H to get the low-degree versions (A^(4))^bm x_H : mathbb R^D to mathbb R^k and (B^(4))^bm y_H : mathbb R^D to mathbb R^k. This guarantees that (A^(4))^bm x_H and (B^(4))^bm y_H have degree at most d. Moreover, we have that for every i, j in [k], inabsinangle(A^(4)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(4)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D - inangle(A^(3)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(3)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D ~le~ delta Additionally, \[ norm2R(A^(4)) - A^(4) ~le~ delta \ and \ norm2R(B^(4)) - B^(4) ~le~ delta \] item Multilinearization: We apply Creflem:multilin_main on (A^(4))^bm x_H and (B^(4))^bm y_H to get the multilinearized and low-influential versions (A^(5))^bm x_H : mathbb R^D_1 to mathbb R^k and (B^(5))^bm y_H : mathbb R^D_1 to mathbb R^k (where D_1 = Dt). Thus, we have for every i, j in [k], \[ inabsinangle(A^(5)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(5)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D_1 - inangle(A^(4)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(4)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D ~le~ delta \] Additionally, combining with Creflem:close-to-simplex, \[ norm2R(A^(5)) - A^(5) ~le~ norm2R(A^(4)) - A^(4) + norm2A^(5) - A^(4) ~le~ 2delta \] Similarly, \[ norm2R(B^(5)) - B^(5) ~le~ 2delta \] Combining all this with Creflem:close-strategies we get that, inabsinangleR_iinparen(A^(5))^bm x_H, R_jinparen(B^(5))^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D_1 - inangle(A^(4)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(4)_j)^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D ~le~ 5delta Additionally, note that we also have that Inf_ell((A^(5)_i))^bm x_H le tau and Inf_ell((B^(5)_i))^bm y_H le tau for all i in [k] and ell in [n]. This is helpful for us to apply the invariance principle next. item Invariance Principle (from mathbb R to Z): We apply Creflem:our_invariance on (A^(5))^bm x_H and (B^(5))^bm y_H to get functions (A^(6))^bm x_H : Z^D_1 to Delta_k and (B^(6))^bm y_H : Z^D_1 to Delta_k, such that for every i, j in [k], inabsinangle(A^(6)_i)^bm x_H, (B^(6)_j)^bm y_H_mu^otimes D_1 - inangleR_iinparen(A^(5))^bm x_H, R_jinparen(B^(5))^bm y_H_G_rho^otimes D_1 ~le~ delta Note again that strictly speaking Creflem:our_invariance gives us functions mapping to mathbb R^k and not Delta_k. However, we consider their rounded versions, which exactly gives us the statement above. paragraphPutting it together. We now show how to put together Crefeqn:NIS-1,eqn:NIS-2,eqn:NIS-3,eqn:NIS-4,eqn:NIS-5,eqn:NIS-6 to get our final conclusion. We now define our final functions wtildeA : Z^n_0 to Delta_k and wtildeB : Z^n_0 to Delta_k as follows. Firstly, we interpret the n_0 = h + D_1 coordinates of bm x as two parts: head coordinates bm x_H in Z^h and the remaining coordinates bm x_R in Z^D_1. Similarly for bm y. \[ wtildeA(bm x) = wtildeA(bm x_H, bm x_R) = (A^(6))^bm x_H(bm x_R) \ and \ wtildeB(bm y) = wtildeB(bm y_H, bm y_R) = (B^(6))^bm y_H(bm y_R)\;.\] We now show that for all i, j in [k], it holds that, \[ inabsinanglewtildeA_i, wtildeB_j_mu^otimes n_0 - nodes.statement: It is well-known that the distribution of norm2bm w follows a chi-distribution with parameter D, and whose probability density function is given by f_D(x) = fracx^D-1 cdot e^- fracx^222^fracD2 - 1 cdot Gamma(fracD2), for every x geq 0 (and where Gamma(cdot) denotes the Gamma function). Thus, we have that E_bm wbigg[frac1\|bm w\|^dbigg] &= int_0^infty frac1x^d cdot f_D(x) dx\\ &= int_0^infty fracx^D-d-1 cdot e^- fracx^222^fracD2 - 1 cdot Gamma(fracD2) dx\\ &= frac2^fracD-d-12 cdot GammainparenfracD-d22^fracD2 - 1 cdot Gamma(fracD2)\\ &= frac1D^d/2 cdot inparen1 pm Oinparenfracd^2D, where the last equality follows from the following Stirling's approximation of the Gamma function, which holds for every real number z > 0: \[ Gamma(z+1) = sqrt 2 pi z cdot inparenfracze^z cdot inparen1 pm Oinparenfrac1z. \] This completes the proof of Crefeq:mean_univ_bd, for the explicit constant C that can be derived from the Stirling's approximation. Now, Crefeq:var_univ_bd immediately follows as: Var_bm winsquarefrac1\| bm w \|^d &~=~ E_bm w insquarefrac1\|bm w\|^2d - E_bm winsquarefrac1\|bm w\|^d^2\\ &~=~ inparenfrac1D^d pm C cdot inparenfrac(2d)^2D^d+1 - inparenfrac1D^d/2 pm C cdot inparenfracd^2D^d/2+1^2\\ &~le~ 8C cdot inparenfracd^2D^d+1, where, we use that D is sufficiently large that C^2 inparenfracd^4D^d+2 < 2C cdot inparenfracd^2D^d+1, i.e. D > Cd^2.

nodes.name: Proof of \Cref{le:corr_norms_rec_ex}
nodes.statement: More specifically, we will show that, inabsEbigg[prodlimits_i=1^ell frac1\|bm w_i\|_2^d_ibigg] - frac1D^d/2 &~le~ C cdot ell^3 cdot bigg(fracd^2D^fracd2+1 bigg) \\ Varinsquareprodlimits_i=1^ell frac1\|bm w_i\|_2^d_i &~le~ 8C cdot ell^3 cdot inparenfracd^2D^d+1 where C is the absolute constant (as obtained in Crefprop:inv_chi_mom_dist). This implies the lemma since ell le d. We proceed by induction on ell (more specifically on log ell). For ell = 1, the bound immediately follows from Crefprop:inv_chi_mom_dist. For the inductive step, we assume that the bound in Crefeq:exp_prod_dep,eq:exp_prod_dep_var holds for ell, and we prove that the bound also holds for 2ell. While it may seem that our bounds are being proven only when ell is a power of 2, it is not hard to see that our proof could be done for non powers of 2 as well, giving a bound that is monotonically increasing in ell and hence it suffices having proved it for ell that are powers of 2. Let d_1, d_2, dots, d_2ell be non-negative integers with d:= sum_i=1^2ell d_i. For notational convenience, let s_1 = sum_i=1^ell d_i and s_2 = sum_i=ell+1^2ell d_i, and so d = s_1 + s_2. We will first prove Crefeq:exp_prod_dep. The main idea that we use to prove this inductively is: for any two random variables X and Y, it holds that E[XY] - E[X] E[Y] = Cov[X,Y], and that the covariance satisfies |Cov[X,Y]| le sqrtVar[X] cdot Var[Y] (by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality). Thus, we get, &Ebigg[prod_i=1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i bigg] ~=~ Ebigg[prod_i=1^ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i \ cdot \ prod_i=ell+1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i bigg]nonumber\\ &~=~ Ebigg[prod_i=1^ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i bigg] cdot Ebigg[ prod_i=ell+1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_ibigg] ~+~ Covbigg[prod_i=1^ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i , prod_i=ell+1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i bigg] nonumber\\ &~=~ Ebigg[prod_i=1^ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i bigg] cdot Ebigg[ prod_i=ell+1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_ibigg] ~pm~ sqrtVarbigg[prod_i=1^ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i bigg] cdot Varbigg[ prod_i=ell+1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_ibigg]\;. Using the inductive assumption w.r.t. ell, we get that, Ebigg[ prod_i=1^ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_ibigg] &~=~ frac1D^s_1/2 inparen1 pm C cdot ell^3 cdot bigg(fracs_1^2D bigg) \\ Ebigg[ prod_i=ell+1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_ibigg] &~=~ frac1D^s_2/2 inparen1 pm C cdot ell^3 cdot bigg(fracs_2^2D bigg) and Varbigg[ prod_i=1^ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_ibigg] &~le~ frac1D^s_1 cdot 8C cdot ell^3 cdot bigg(fracs_1^2D bigg) \\ Varbigg[ prod_i=ell+1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_ibigg] &~le~ frac1D^s_2 cdot 8C cdot ell^3 cdot bigg(fracs_2^2D bigg) Plugging Crefeq:exp_ind1,eq:exp_ind2,eq:var_ind1,eq:var_ind2 in Crefeq:cov_manip, it is not hard to see that, Ebigg[prod_i=1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i bigg] = frac1D^d/2 inparen1 pm C cdot (2ell)^3 cdot bigg(fracd^2D bigg)\;. This completes the proof of Crefeq:exp_prod_dep. Now, Crefeq:exp_prod_dep_var follows easily as, Varinsquareprod_i=1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i &~=~ E insquareprod_i=1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^2d_i - E_bm winsquareprod_i=1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i^2\\ &~=~ inparenfrac1D^d pm C cdot (2ell)^3 inparenfrac(2d)^2D^d+1 - inparenfrac1D^d/2 pm C cdot (2ell)^3 cdot inparenfracd^2D^d/2+1^2\\ &~le~ 8C cdot (2ell)^3 cdot inparenfracd^2D^d+1\;.

This completes the proof of Crefeq:exp_prod_dep. Now, Crefeq:exp_prod_dep_var follows easily as, Varinsquareprod_i=1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i &~=~ E insquareprod_i=1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^2d_i - E_bm winsquareprod_i=1^2ell frac1norm2bm w_i^d_i^2\\ &~=~ inparenfrac1D^d pm C cdot (2ell)^3 inparenfrac(2d)^2D^d+1 - inparenfrac1D^d/2 pm C cdot (2ell)^3 cdot inparenfracd^2D^d/2+1^2\\ &~le~ 8C cdot (2ell)^3 cdot inparenfracd^2D^d+1\;.

More specifically we will show that when $\ell$ is a power of $2$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:mag_bd_mult_Gauss}
	\bigg|  \mathbb{E} \bigg[ \prod_{i=1}^{\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] \bigg| \le 2^{\ell-1} (\ell d)^{d}.
	\end{equation}
	It is easy to see that this immediately implies the bound of $2^d \cdot d^{2d}$ in the main lemma, since $\ell \le d$. However if $\ell$ is not a power of $2$ we can round it up to the nearest power of $2$, which amounts to substituting $\ell \le 2d$ in the above, obtaining a bound of $2^{3d} \cdot d^{2d} \le (2d)^{3d}$.\\
	
	\noindent We proceed by induction on $\ell$ (more specifically on $\log \ell$). For $\ell = 1$, we use the well-known fact that for $w \sim \gamma_1$,
	$$\inabs{\mathbb{E}[w^d]} ~=~ \inbrace{\inmat{0 & \ \mathrm{if} \ d \text{ is odd} \\ (d-1)!! & \ \mathrm{if} \ d \text{ is even}}} ~\le~ d^{d},$$
	where $(d-1)!!$ denotes the double factorial of $(d-1)$, i.e., the product of all integers from $1$ to $d-1$ that have the same parity as $d-1$. For the inductive step, we assume that the bound in (\ref{eq:mag_bd_mult_Gauss}) holds for $\ell$ and we show that it also holds for $2\ell$. For notational convenience, let $s_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} d_i$ and $s_2 = \sum_{i=\ell+1}^{2\ell} d_i$, and so $d = s_1 + s_2$.
	
	The main idea that we use to prove the inductive step is: for any two random variables $X$ and $Y$, it holds that $\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X] \mathbb{E}[Y] + \mathsf{Cov}[X,Y]$, and that the covariance satisfies $|\mathsf{Cov}[X,Y]| \le \sqrt{\mathsf{Var}[X] \cdot \mathsf{Var}[Y]}$ (by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality). Additionally, we use that $\mathsf{Var}[X] \le \mathbb{E}[X^2]$. Thus, we get,
	\begin{align*}
	&\bigg|  \mathbb{E} \bigg[ \prod_{i=1}^{2\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] \bigg|
	~=~ \bigg|  \mathbb{E} \bigg[ \prod_{i=1}^{\ell} w_i^{d_i} \cdot \prod_{i=\ell+1}^{2\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] \bigg|\\
	&~=~ \bigg|  \mathbb{E}\bigg[ \prod_{i=1}^{\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] \cdot \mathbb{E} \bigg[ \prod_{i=\ell+1}^{2\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] ~+~ \mathsf{Cov}\bigg[ \prod_{i=1}^{\ell} w_i^{d_i}\ , \prod_{i=\ell+1}^{2\ell} w_i^{d_i}\bigg]  \bigg| \\ 
	&~\le~ \bigg|  \mathbb{E}\bigg[ \prod_{i=1}^{\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] \cdot \mathbb{E} \bigg[ \prod_{i=\ell+1}^{2\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] \bigg|  ~+~ \sqrt{\mathsf{Var}\bigg[ \prod_{i=1}^{\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] \cdot \mathsf{Var}\bigg[ \prod_{i=\ell+1}^{2\ell} w_i^{d_i}\bigg]}\\
	&~\le~ \bigg|  \mathbb{E}\bigg[ \prod_{i=1}^{\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] \cdot \mathbb{E} \bigg[ \prod_{i=\ell+1}^{2\ell} w_i^{d_i} \bigg] \bigg| ~+~ \sqrt{\mathbb{E}\bigg[ \prod_{i=1}^{\ell} w_i^{2d_i} \bigg] \cdot \mathbb{E}\bigg[ \prod_{i=\ell+1}^{2\ell} w_i^{2d_i}\bigg]}\\
	&~\le~ 2^{\ell-1} (\ell s_1)^{s_1} \cdot 2^{\ell-1} (\ell s_2)^{s_2} + \sqrt{2^{\ell - 1} (2\ell s_1)^{2s_1} \cdot 2^{\ell-1} (2\ell s_2)^{2s_2}}\\
	&~\le~ 2^{2\ell-1} (2\ell d)^{d}\;,
	\end{align*}
	where, the second last inequality uses the inductive assumption regarding product of $\ell$ terms. The last inequality follows from $s_1^{s_1} \cdot s_2^{s_2} \le d^{s_1} \cdot d^{s_2} = d^d$.

nodes.statement: Let S subseteq [D]^d be the set of all tuples bm c in [D]^d such that c_j neq c_k for all j neq k in [d]. Let overlineS denote the complement of S in [D]^d. Note that |overlineS| le d^2 cdot D^d-1. We have that Ebigg[ prod_i=1^d langle bm u_i, bm v_i rangle bigg] &~=~ Ebigg[ prod_i=1^d sum_k=1^D u_i,k v_i,k bigg] nonumber \\ &~=~ E bigg[ sum_bm c in [D]^d prod_i=1^d u_i, c_i v_i, c_i bigg] nonumber \\ &~=~ sum_bm c in [D]^d E bigg[ prod_i=1^d u_i, c_i v_i, c_i bigg] nonumber \\ &~=~ sum_bm c in S E bigg[ prod_i=1^d u_i, c_i v_i, c_i bigg] + sum_bm c in overlineS E bigg[ prod_i=1^d u_i, c_i v_i, c_i bigg] nonumber\\ &~=~ sum_bm c in S prod_i=1^d E[ u_i, c_i v_i, c_i] + sum_bm c in overlineS E bigg[ prod_i=1^d u_i, c_i v_i, c_i bigg], where the last equality follows from the assumption that the distribution of (u_1,j, ldots, u_d,j, v_1,j, ldots, v_d,j) is independent across j in [D]. nodes.name: Proof of \Cref{le:norm_Gauss}
nodes.statement: We prove this lemma in two steps. We show the following two bounds, inabsElimits_setbm u_i, bm v_i_i \ insquareprod_i=1^d fracinanglebm u_i, bm v_inorm2bm u_i norm2bm v_i - Elimits_setbm u_i, bm v_i_i \ insquareprod_i=1^d fracinanglebm u_i, bm v_iD &~le~ Oinparenfracd^2.5sqrtD + fracd^O(d)D. \\ inabsElimits_setbm u_i, bm v_i_i \ insquareprod_i=1^d fracinanglebm u_i, bm v_iD - prod_i=1^d \ Elimits_setbm a_i, bm b_i_i \ insquarefracinanglebm u_i, bm v_iD &~le~ fracd^O(d)D. Crefle:norm_Gauss now follows immediately by the triangle inequality, for an explicit choice of D that is upper bounded by fracd^O(d)delta^2.\\ Note that Crefeq:unorm_ineq_norms is simply a restatement of Crefle:swap_exp_prod. To prove Crefeq:norm_ineq_norms, we define the random variables \[ W ~:=~ prod_i=1^d inanglebm u_i, bm v_i \ and \ Z ~:=~ prod_i=1^d frac1norm2bm u_i norm2bm v_i ~-~ frac1D^d\;. \] Note that Crefeq:norm_ineq_norms is equivalent to showing bounds on |E[W cdot Z]|. In order to do so, we show the following four bounds: item inabsE[W] = D^d + d^O(d) cdot D^d-1. item Var[W] = D^2d + d^O(d) cdot D^2d-1. item inabsE[Z] = Oinparenfracd^5D^d+1. item Var[Z] = Oinparenfracd^5D^2d+1. We now prove each of these four bounds. We start by proving Crefit:W_mean. By Crefle:swap_exp_prod, we have that |E[W]| &~le~ bigg| prod_i=1^d E [ langle bm u_i, bm v_i rangle ] bigg| + d^O(d) cdot D^d-1\\ &~=~ bigg| prod_i=1^d sum_j=1^D E[bm u_i,j bm v_i,j] bigg| + d^O(d) cdot D^d-1\\ &~le~ D^d + d^O(d) cdot D^d-1 To prove Crefit:W_var, we can again apply Crefle:swap_exp_prod as follows: Var[W] &~le~ E[W^2]\\ &~=~ E insquareprod_i=1^d inanglebm u_i, bm v_i^2\\ &~le~ D^2d + d^O(d) cdot D^2d-1 Finally, we note that Crefit:Z_mean,it:Z_var follows exactly from Crefle:corr_norms_rec_ex.\\ To put this together, recall the definition of covariance Cov[W,Z] := E[W cdot Z] - E[W] cdot E[Z], and that by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, |Cov[W,Z]| le sqrtVar[W] cdot Var[Z]. Thus, inabsE[W cdot Z] &= inabsE[W] cdot E[Z] + Cov(W,Z)\\ &~le~ inabsE[W] cdot E[Z] + inabsCov(W,Z)\\ &~le~ inabsE[W] cdot inabsE[Z] + sqrtVar[W] cdot Var[Z]\\ &~le~ Oinparenfracd^2.5sqrtD + fracd^O(d)D where the last line combines Crefit:W_mean,it:W_var,it:Z_mean,it:Z_var.

We have that
	\begin{align}\label{eq:mean_manip}
		\mathbb{E}_{M} \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \mathbf{U}_S \mathbf{V}_T &~=~ \mathbb{E}_{M} \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \bigg[ \prod_{i \in S} U_i  \cdot \prod_{i \in T} V_i \bigg]\nonumber\\ 
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \mathbb{E}_{M} \bigg[  \prod_{i \in S \cap T} U_i V_i \cdot \prod_{i \in S \setminus T} U_i \cdot \prod_{i \in T \setminus S} V_i  \bigg]\nonumber\\ 
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \mathbb{E}_{M} \bigg[  \prod_{i \in S \cap T} \inangle{{\bm m}_i, \wtilde{{\bm a}}} \inangle{{\bm m}_i , \wtilde{{\bm b}}} \cdot \prod_{i \in S \setminus T} \inangle{{\bm m}_i, \wtilde{{\bm a}}} \cdot \prod_{i \in T \setminus S} \inangle{{\bm m}_i , \wtilde{{\bm b}}} \bigg]\nonumber\\ 
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \bigg[\prod_{i \in S \cap T} \mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}_i} \inangle{{\bm m}_i, \wtilde{{\bm a}}} \inangle{{\bm m}_i , \wtilde{{\bm b}}} \cdot \prod_{i \in S \setminus T} \mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}_i} \inangle{{\bm m}_i, \wtilde{{\bm a}}} \cdot \prod_{i \in T \setminus S} \mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}_i} \inangle{{\bm m}_i , \wtilde{{\bm b}}} \bigg],
	\end{align}
	where the last equality follows from the independence of the ${\bm m}_i$'s.\\
	
	\noindent If $S \neq T$, then either $S \setminus T$ is non-empty in which case $\prod_{i \in S \setminus T} \mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}_i}[\inangle{{\bm m}_i, \wtilde{{\bm a}}}] = 0$ or $T \setminus S$ is non-empty in which case $\prod_{i \in T \setminus S} \mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}_i}[\inangle{{\bm m}_i , \wtilde{{\bm b}}}] = 0$.  This is because for any fixed vector ${\bm a}$ and for each $i \in [N]$, the random variable $\inangle{{\bm m}_i, \wtilde{{\bm a}}}$ has zero-mean (and similarly for $\inangle{{\bm m}_i, \wtilde{{\bm b}}}$). The first part of the lemma now follows from \Cref{eq:mean_manip}.\\
	
	\noindent If $S = T$, \Cref{eq:mean_manip} becomes
	\begin{align*}
		\mathbb{E}_{M} \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \mathbf{U}_S \mathbf{V}_T
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \bigg[ \prod_{i \in S} \mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}_i}\frac{\langle {\bm m}_i, {\bm a} \rangle}{\|{\bm a}\|_2} \frac{\langle {\bm m}_i , {\bm b} \rangle}{\|{\bm b}\|_2} \bigg]\\
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \bigg[\prod_{i \in S} \frac{ \langle {\bm a}, {\bm b} \rangle}{\|{\bm a}\|_2 \|{\bm b}\|_2} \bigg] \qquad \insquare{\text{since $\mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}_i} {\bm m}_i \cdot {\bm m}_i^T = I_{D \times D}$.}}\\
		&~=~ \prod_{i \in S} \bigg[ \frac{ \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}}\langle {\bm a}, {\bm b} \rangle}{D} \bigg] \pm \delta\\
		&~=~ \rho^{|S|} \pm \delta,
	\end{align*}
	where the penultimate equality above follows from \Cref{le:norm_Gauss} for an explicit choice of $D$ that is upper bounded by $\frac{d^{O(d)}}{\delta^2}$.

\label{lem:var_bound_monomial}
	Given parameters $d$ and $\delta$, there exists an explicitly computable $D := D(d, \delta)$ such that the following holds:
	For any subsets $S, T, S', T' \subseteq [N]$ satisfying $|S|, |T|, |S'|, |T'| \le d$, it holds that,
	\begin{align*}
		\text{if } \ S \triangle T \triangle S' \triangle T' \ne \emptyset ~:~
		& \ \inabs{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{\mathbf{U}_S \mathbf{V}_T \mathbf{U}'_{S'} \mathbf{V}'_{T'}} - \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \insquare{\mathbf{U}_S \mathbf{V}_T}} \cdot \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{\mathbf{U}'_{S'} \mathbf{V}'_{T'}}}} ~=~ 0\;,\\
		\text{if }\ S \triangle T \triangle S' \triangle T' = \emptyset ~:~
		& \ \inabs{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{\mathbf{U}_S \mathbf{V}_T \mathbf{U}'_{S'} \mathbf{V}'_{T'}} - \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \insquare{\mathbf{U}_S \mathbf{V}_T}} \cdot \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{\mathbf{U}'_{S'} \mathbf{V}'_{T'}}}} ~\le~ \delta.
	\end{align*}
	Here, $S \triangle T \triangle S' \triangle T'$ is the symmetric difference of the sets $S, T, S', T'$, equivalently, the set of all $i \in [N]$ which appear an odd number of times in the multiset $S \sqcup T \sqcup S' \sqcup T'$.\\
	In particular, one may take $D = \frac{d^{O(d)}}{\delta^2}$.

To prove the first part of the lemma, consider the quantity
	\begin{align*}
		T({\bm a}, {\bm b}, {\bm a}', {\bm b}') &~:=~  \mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}}[ \inangle{ {\bm m}, \wtilde{{\bm a}} } \inangle{ {\bm m}, \wtilde{{\bm b}} } \inangle{ {\bm m}, \wtilde{{\bm a}}' } \inangle{ {\bm m}, \wtilde{{\bm b}}'}] - \mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}}[\inangle{ {\bm m}, \wtilde{{\bm a}} } \inangle{ m , \wtilde{{\bm b}} } ] \cdot \mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}}[\inangle{ m, \wtilde{{\bm a}}' } \inangle{ {\bm m}, \wtilde{{\bm b}}' }]\\ 
		&~=~ \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm b}} } \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}}', \wtilde{{\bm b}}' } + \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm a}}' } \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm b}}, \wtilde{{\bm b}}' } + \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm b}}' } \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}}', \wtilde{{\bm b}} } - \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm b}} } \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}}' , \wtilde{{\bm b}}' }\\ 
		&~=~ \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm a}}' } \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm b}}, \wtilde{{\bm b}}' } + \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm b}}' } \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}}', \wtilde{{\bm b}} }.
	\end{align*}
	where we use that for any $i \in [D]$, it holds that $\mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}} [m_i^4] = 3$ and $\mathbb{E}_{{\bm m}} [m_i^2] = 1$.
	Thus,
	\begin{align*}
		\mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}, {\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{T({\bm a}, {\bm b}, {\bm a}', {\bm b}')^2} &~=~\mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}, {\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{ \insquare{\inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm a}}' } \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm b}}, \wtilde{{\bm b}}' } + \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm b}}' } \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}}', \wtilde{{\bm b}} } }^2 }\\ 
		&~\le~ 2 \cdot \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}, {\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{ \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm a}}' }^2 \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm b}}, \wtilde{{\bm b}}' }^2} ~+~ 2 \cdot \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}, {\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{ \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}} , \wtilde{{\bm b}}' }^2 \inangle{ \wtilde{{\bm a}}', \wtilde{{\bm b}} }^2 }\\ 
		&~\le~ O \inparen{\frac{1}{D^2}},
	\end{align*}
	where the last step follows by two applications of \Cref{le:norm_Gauss} (with $d = 4$). This completes the proof of the first part of the lemma. nodes.statement: Let 1(E) denote the 0/1 indicator function of an event E. We have that Elimits_M Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquareU_S V_T U'_S' V'_T' &= Elimits_M Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquare prod_i in S cup T cup S' cup T' U_i^1(i in S) V_i^1(i in T) U'_i^1(i in S') V'_i^1(i in T') nonumber \\ &= Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquare prod_i in S cup T cup S' cup T' Elimits_bm m_i insquare U_i^1(i in S) V_i^1(i in T) U'_i^1(i in S') V'_i^1(i in T'). On the other hand, we have that Elimits_M Elimits_bm a, bm b insquareU_S V_T &= Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_M insquare prod_i in S cup T U_i^1(i in S) V_i^1(i in T) = Elimits_bm a, bm b insquare prod_i in S cup T E_bm m_i insquareU_i^1(i in S) V_i^1(i in T), and similarly Elimits_M Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquareU'_S' V'_T' &= Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquare prod_i in S' cup T' E_bm m_i insquareU_i^1(i in S') V_i^1(i in T'). If there exists i in S cup T cup S' cup T' that appears in an odd number of S, T, S' and T', then it can be seen that the expectation in Crefeq:joint is equal to 0, and that at least one of the expectations in Crefeq:first_ind,eq:sec_ind is equal to 0. This already handles the case that S triangle T triangle S' triangle T' ne emptyset. Henceforth, we assume that each i in S cup T cup S' cup T' appears in an even number of S, T, S' and T'. Assume for ease of notation that S cup T cup S' cup T' subseteq [4d]. Define g_i(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b') &~:=~ E_bm m_i insquareU_i^1(i in S) V_i^1(i in T) U'_i^1(i in S') V'_i^1(i in T') \\ h_i(bm a, bm b) &~:=~ E_bm m_i insquareU_i^1(i in S) V_i^1(i in T).\\ h_i'(bm a', bm b') &~:=~ E_bm m_i insquareU_i'^1(i in S') V_i'^1(i in T'). Combining Crefeq:joint,eq:first_ind,eq:sec_ind along with the definitions in Crefeq:g_function,eq:h_function,eq:h'_function, we get & bigg| Elimits_M Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquareU_S V_T U'_S' V'_T' - Elimits_M Elimits_bm a, bm b insquareU_S V_T cdot Elimits_M Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquareU'_S' V'_T' bigg|\\ &~=~ bigg|Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquare prod_i = 1^4 d g_i(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b') - prod_i = 1^4 d h_i(bm a, bm b) cdot h_i'(bm a', bm b')bigg|\\ &~=~ bigg|Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquare sum_j=1^4d insquare prod_i = 1^j-1 h_i(bm a, bm b) cdot h_i'(bm a', bm b') prod_i = j^4d g_i(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b') - prod_i = 1^j h_i(bm a, bm b) cdot h_i'(bm a', bm b') prod_i = j+1^4d g_i(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b')bigg|\\ &~le~ sum_j=1^4d \ bigg|Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquare prod_i = 1^j-1 h_i(bm a, bm b) cdot h_i'(bm a', bm b') prod_i = j+1^4d g_i(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b') cdot insquareg_j(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b') - h_j(bm a, bm b) cdot h_j'(bm a', bm b')bigg|\\ &~le~ 4 cdot d cdot sqrttau cdot kappa, where the last inequality follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality with tau &~:=~ max_j in [4d] ~Elimits_bm a, bm b ~Elimits_bm a', bm b' ~insquare prod_i = 1^j-1 h_i(bm a, bm b)^2 cdot h_i(bm a', bm b')^2 prod_i = j+1^4d g_i(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b')^2 \\ kappa &~:=~ max_j in [4d] ~Elimits_bm a, bm b ~Elimits_bm a', bm b' ~insquareg_j(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b') - h_j(bm a, bm b) cdot h_j(bm a', bm b')^2 Crefle:square implies that kappa le O(1/D). We now show that tau le 2^O(d). Note that for any i in [D], it holds that, \[ h_i(bm a, bm b) ~=~ inforkinanglewtildebm a, wtildebm b & \ if \ i in S \ and \ i in T\\ 1 & \ if \ i notin S \ and \ i notin T \\ 0 & otherwise \ and \ h_i'(bm a', bm b') ~=~ inforkinanglewtildebm a', wtildebm b' & \ if \ i in S' \ and \ i in T'\\ 1 & \ if \ i notin S' \ and \ i notin T' \\ 0 & otherwise \] \[ g_i(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b') ~=~ infork inanglewtildebm a, wtildebm binanglewtildebm a', wtildebm b' + inanglewtildebm a, wtildebm a'inanglewtildebm b, wtildebm b' + inanglewtildebm a, wtildebm b'inanglewtildebm a', wtildebm b & \ if \ i in S cap T cap S' cap T' \\ inanglewtildebm a, wtildebm b & \ if \ i in S cap T \ and \ i notin S' cup T' \\ inanglewtildebm a, wtildebm a' & \ if \ i in S cap S' \ and \ i notin T cup T' \\ inanglewtildebm a, wtildebm b' & \ if \ i in S cap T' \ and \ i notin S' cup T \\ inanglewtildebm a', wtildebm b & \ if \ i in S' cap T \ and \ i notin S cup T' \\ inanglewtildebm a', wtildebm b' & \ if \ i in S' cap T' \ and \ i notin S cup T \\ inanglewtildebm b, wtildebm b' & \ if \ i in T cap T' \ and \ i notin S cup S' \\ 1 & otherwise \] Thus, if we expand out a single term prod_i = 1^j-1 h_i(bm a, bm b)^2 cdot h_i(bm a', bm b')^2 prod_i = j+1^4d g_i(bm a, bm b, bm a', bm b')^2, we get at most 3^8d terms (since each g_i can multiply the number of terms by at most 3). Each of these terms is the expectation of the product of inner product of some correlated Gaussian vectors. We thus have from Crefle:norm_Gauss that each such term is at most 1 + delta. Thus, we have that tau le 2^O(d). For an explicit choice of D that is upper bounded by d^O(d)/delta^2, we get that 4 d sqrttau kappa le delta, which concludes the proof of the lemma.

nodes.statement: Creflem:mean_var_bound We start out by proving the bound on inabsE_M F(M) - inangleA, B_G_rho^otimes N. To this end, we will use Creflem:mean_bound_monomial with parameters d and delta. Thus, for a choice of D = d^O(d)/delta^2, we have that, & inabsE_M F(M) - inangleA, B_G_rho^otimes N\\ &~=~ inabsElimits_M \ Elimits_bm a, bm b insquareA(U) cdot B(V) - Elimits_X, Y sim G_rho^otimes N insquareA(X) cdot B(Y)\\ &~=~ inabssumlimits_S, T subseteq [N] whatA_S whatB_T cdot inparenElimits_M \ Elimits_bm a, bm b insquareU_S cdot V_T - E_X, Y sim G_rho^otimes N insquareX_S cdot Y_T\\ &~=~ inabssumlimits_S subseteq [N] whatA_S whatB_S cdot inparenElimits_M \ Elimits_bm a, bm b insquareU_S cdot V_S - rho^|S| ldots \ (terms corresponding to S ne T are 0.)\\ &~le~ sumlimits_S subseteq [N] inabswhatA_S whatB_S cdot delta ldots ldots \ (using Creflem:mean_bound_monomial)\\ &~le~ norm2A cdot norm2B cdot delta ldots ldots \ (Cauchy-Schwarz inequality)\\ &~le~ delta ldots ldots \ (norm2A, norm2B le 1)qedhere We now move to proving the bound on Var_M(F(M)). To this end, we will use Creflem:var_bound_monomial with parameters d and delta/9^d. Thus, for a choice of D = d^O(d)/delta^2, we have that, & E_M inparenE_bm a, bm b A(U) cdot B(V)^2 - inparenE_M E_bm a, bm b A(U) cdot B(V)^2\\ & ~=~inabsElimits_M Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquareA(U) B(V) A(U') B(V') - inparenElimits_M Elimits_bm a, bm b insquareA(U) B(V) cdot inparenElimits_M Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquareA(U') B(V')\\ & ~le~ sum_substackS, T subseteq [N] \\ S', T' subseteq [N] inabswhatA_S whatB_T whatA_S' whatB_T' cdot inabsElimits_M Elimits_bm a, bm b Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquareU_S V_T U'_S' V'_T' - inparenElimits_M Elimits_bm a, bm b insquareU_S V_T cdot inparenElimits_M Elimits_bm a', bm b' insquareU'_S' V'_T'\\ & ~le~ fracdelta9^d cdot sum_substackS, T, S', T' subseteq [N] \\ S triangle T triangle S' triangle T' = emptyset inabswhatA_S whatB_T whatA_S' whatB_T'\;. To finish the proof, we will show that, \[sum_substackS, T, S', T' subseteq [N] \\ S triangle T triangle S' triangle T' = emptyset inabswhatA_S whatB_T whatA_S' whatB_T' ~le~ 9^d cdot norm2A^2 cdot norm2B^2\;.\] Define functions f : set1, -1^N to mathbb R, g : set1, -1^N to mathbb R over the boolean hypercube as, \[f(x) = sum_substackS subseteq [N] \\ |S| le d whatA_S X_S(x) \ and \ g(x) = sum_substackS subseteq [N] \\ |S| le d whatB_S X_S(x)\;.\] Hypercontractivity bounds for degree-d polynomials over the boolean hypercube imply that, \[E_x insquaref(x)^4 le 9^d inparenE_x insquaref(x)^2^2 \ and \ E_x insquareg(x)^4 le 9^d inparenE_x insquareg(x)^2^2\;.\] We now finish the proof as follows, sum_substackS, T, S', T' subseteq [N] \\ S triangle T triangle S' triangle T' = emptyset inabswhatA_S whatB_T whatA_S' whatB_T' &~=~ E_x insquaref(x)^2 g(x)^2\\ &~le~ inparenE_x insquaref(x)^4^1/2 cdot inparenE_x insquareg(x)^4^1/2\\ &~le~ 9^d cdot inparenE_x insquaref(x)^2 cdot inparenE_x insquareg(x)^2\\ &~=~ 9^d cdot inparensum_S whatA_S^2 cdot inparensum_S whatB_S^2\\ &~=~ 9^d cdot norm2A^2 cdot norm2B^2. Thus, overall we get that, Var_M(F(M)) le delta.\\ This completes the proof of Creflem:mean_var_bound for an explicit choice of D that is upper bounded by d^O(d)/delta^2.

{\Cref{lem:mean_var_bound}}
	We start out by proving the bound on $\inabs{\mathbb{E}_{M} F(M) - \inangle{A, B}_{\mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes N}}}$. To this end, we will use \Cref{lem:mean_bound_monomial} with parameters $d$ and $\delta$. Thus, for a choice of $D = d^{O(d)}/\delta^2$, we have that,
	\begin{align*}
		& \inabs{\mathbb{E}_{M} F(M) - \inangle{A, B}_{\mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes N}}}\\
		&~=~ \inabs{\mathbb{E}\limits_M \ \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \insquare{A(\mathbf{U}) \cdot B(\mathbf{V})} - \mathbb{E}\limits_{\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \sim \mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes N}} \insquare{A(\mathbf{X}) \cdot B(\mathbf{Y})}}\\
		&~=~ \inabs{\sum\limits_{S, T \subseteq [N]} \what{A}_S \what{B}_T \cdot \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_M \ \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \insquare{\mathbf{U}_S \cdot \mathbf{V}_T} - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \sim \mathcal{G}_{\rho}^{\otimes N}} \insquare{\mathbf{X}_S \cdot \mathbf{Y}_T}}}\\
		&~=~ \inabs{\sum\limits_{S \subseteq [N]} \what{A}_S \what{B}_S \cdot \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_M \ \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \insquare{\mathbf{U}_S \cdot \mathbf{V}_S} - \rho^{|S|}}} \qquad \ldots \ \text{(terms corresponding to $S \ne T$ are $0$.)}\\
		&~\le~ \sum\limits_{S \subseteq [N]} \inabs{\what{A}_S \what{B}_S} \cdot \delta \qquad \qquad \ldots \ldots \ \text{(using \Cref{lem:mean_bound_monomial})}\\
		&~\le~ \norm{2}{A} \cdot \norm{2}{B} \cdot \delta \qquad \qquad \ldots \ldots \ \text{(Cauchy-Schwarz inequality)}\\
		&~\le~ \delta \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \ldots \ldots \ \text{($\norm{2}{A}, \norm{2}{B} \le 1$)}\qedhere
	\end{align*}
	We now move to proving the bound on $\mathsf{Var}_M(F(M))$. To this end, we will use \Cref{lem:var_bound_monomial} with parameters $d$ and $\delta/9^d$. Thus, for a choice of $D = d^{O(d)}/\delta^2$, we have that,
	\begin{align*}
		& \mathbb{E}_M \inparen{\mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} A(\mathbf{U}) \cdot B(\mathbf{V})}^2 - \inparen{\mathbb{E}_M \mathbb{E}_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} A(\mathbf{U}) \cdot B(\mathbf{V})}^2\\
		& ~=~\inabs{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{A(\mathbf{U}) B(\mathbf{V}) A(\mathbf{U}') B(\mathbf{V}')} - \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \insquare{A(\mathbf{U}) B(\mathbf{V})}} \cdot \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{A(\mathbf{U}') B(\mathbf{V}')}}}\\
		& ~\le~ \sum_{\substack{S, T \subseteq [N] \\ S', T' \subseteq [N]}} \inabs{\what{A}_S \what{B}_T \what{A}_{S'} \what{B}_{T'}} \cdot \inabs{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{\mathbf{U}_S \mathbf{V}_T \mathbf{U}'_{S'} \mathbf{V}'_{T'}} - \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}, {\bm b}} \insquare{\mathbf{U}_S \mathbf{V}_T}} \cdot \inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_{M} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm a}', {\bm b}'} \insquare{\mathbf{U}'_{S'} \mathbf{V}'_{T'}}}}\\
		& ~\le~ \frac{\delta}{9^d} \cdot \sum_{\substack{S, T, S', T' \subseteq [N] \\ S \triangle T \triangle S' \triangle T' = \emptyset}} \inabs{\what{A}_S \what{B}_T \what{A}_{S'} \what{B}_{T'}}\;.
	\end{align*}
	To finish the proof, we will show that,
	\[\sum_{\substack{S, T, S', T' \subseteq [N] \\ S \triangle T \triangle S' \triangle T' = \emptyset}} \inabs{\what{A}_S \what{B}_T \what{A}_{S'} \what{B}_{T'}} ~\le~ 9^d \cdot \norm{2}{A}^2 \cdot \norm{2}{B}^2\;.\]
	Define functions $f : \set{1, -1}^N \to {\mathbb R}$, $g : \set{1, -1}^N \to {\mathbb R}$ over the boolean hypercube as,
	\[f(x) = \sum_{\substack{S \subseteq [N] \\ |S| \le d}} \what{A}_S \mathcal{X}_S(x) \quad \ \mathrm{and} \ \quad g(x) = \sum_{\substack{S \subseteq [N] \\ |S| \le d}} \what{B}_S \mathcal{X}_S(x)\;.\]
	Hypercontractivity bounds \cite{wolff2007hypercontractivity} for degree-$d$ polynomials over the boolean hypercube imply that,
	\[\mathbb{E}_x \insquare{f(x)^4} \le 9^d \inparen{\mathbb{E}_x \insquare{f(x)^2}}^2 \quad \ \mathrm{and} \ \quad \mathbb{E}_x \insquare{g(x)^4} \le 9^d \inparen{\mathbb{E}_x \insquare{g(x)^2}}^2\;.\]
	We now finish the proof as follows,
	\begin{align*}
		\sum_{\substack{S, T, S', T' \subseteq [N] \\ S \triangle T \triangle S' \triangle T' = \emptyset}} \inabs{\what{A}_S \what{B}_T \what{A}_{S'} \what{B}_{T'}}
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}_{x} \insquare{f(x)^2 g(x)^2}\\
		&~\le~ \inparen{\mathbb{E}_x \insquare{f(x)^4}}^{1/2} \cdot \inparen{\mathbb{E}_x \insquare{g(x)^4}}^{1/2}\\
		&~\le~ 9^d \cdot \inparen{\mathbb{E}_x \insquare{f(x)^2}} \cdot \inparen{\mathbb{E}_x \insquare{g(x)^2}}\\
		&~=~ 9^d \cdot \inparen{\sum_S \what{A}_S^2} \cdot \inparen{\sum_S \what{B}_S^2}\\
		&~=~ 9^d \cdot \norm{2}{A}^2 \cdot \norm{2}{B}^2.
	\end{align*}
	Thus, overall we get that, $\mathsf{Var}_M(F(M)) \le \delta$.\\
	
	\noindent This completes the proof of \Cref{lem:mean_var_bound} for an explicit choice of $D$ that is upper bounded by $d^{O(d)}/\delta^2$.

nodes.name: Low-degree truncation
nodes.statement: We define this for functions in L^2(Z^n, mu^otimes n) and also for those in L^2(mathbb R^n, gamma_n).\\ Discrete Hypercube: Suppose A in L^2(Z^n, mu^otimes n) is given by the Fourier expansion A(bm x) = sumlimits_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_q^n whatA_boldsymbol sigma X_boldsymbol sigma(bm x). The degree-d truncation of A is defined as the function A^le d in L^2(Z^n, mu^otimes n) given by \[A^le d(bm x) ~:=~ sum_substackboldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_q^n \\ |boldsymbol sigma| le d whatA_boldsymbol sigma X_boldsymbol sigma(bm x).\] That is, A^le d is obtained by retaining only the terms with degree at most d in the Fourier expansion of A, where recall that for boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_q^n, its degree is defined as |boldsymbol sigma| = setdefi in [n]boldsymbol sigma_i ne 0.\\ Gaussian: Suppose A in L^2(mathbb R^n, gamma_n) is given by the Hermite expansion A(X) = sum_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n whatA_boldsymbol sigma H_boldsymbol sigma(X). The degree-d truncation of A is defined as the function A^le d in L^2(mathbb R^n, gamma_n) given by \[A^le d(X) ~:=~ sum_substackboldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n \\ |boldsymbol sigma| le d whatA_boldsymbol sigma H_boldsymbol sigma(X).\] That is, A^le d is obtained by retaining only the terms with degree at most d in the Hermite expansion of A, where recall that for boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n, its degree is defined as |boldsymbol sigma| = sum_i=1^n sigma_i.\\ For convenience, in either case, define A^> d := A - A^le d. Also, for vector valued functions A, we define A^le d as the function obtained by applying the above low-degree truncation on each coordinate.

\label{def:low_deg_truncation}
	We define this for functions in $L^2(\mathcal{Z}^n, \mu^{\otimes n})$ and also for those in $L^2({\mathbb R}^n, \gamma_n)$.\\
	
	\noindent {\bf Discrete Hypercube:} Suppose $A \in L^2(\mathcal{Z}^n, \mu^{\otimes n})$ is given by the Fourier expansion $A({\bm x}) = \sum\limits_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_q^n} \what{A}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}} \mathcal{X}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}({\bm x})$. The {\em degree-$d$ truncation} of $A$ is defined as the function $A^{\le d} \in L^2(\mathcal{Z}^n, \mu^{\otimes n})$ given by
	\[A^{\le d}({\bm x}) ~:=~ \sum_{\substack{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_q^n \\ |{\boldsymbol \sigma}| \le d}} \what{A}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}} \mathcal{X}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}({\bm x}).\]
	That is, $A^{\le d}$ is obtained by retaining only the terms with degree at most $d$ in the Fourier expansion of $A$, where recall that for ${\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_q^n$, its degree is defined as $|{\boldsymbol \sigma}| = \setdef{i \in [n]}{{\boldsymbol \sigma}_i \ne 0}$.\\
	
	\noindent {\bf Gaussian:} Suppose $A \in L^2({\mathbb R}^n, \gamma_n)$ is given by the Hermite expansion $A(\mathbf{X}) = \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n} \what{A}_{\boldsymbol \sigma} H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(\mathbf{X})$. The {\em degree-$d$ truncation} of $A$ is defined as the function $A^{\le d} \in L^2({\mathbb R}^n, \gamma_n)$ given by
	\[A^{\le d}(\mathbf{X}) ~:=~ \sum_{\substack{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n \\ |{\boldsymbol \sigma}| \le d}} \what{A}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}} H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(\mathbf{X}).\]
	That is, $A^{\le d}$ is obtained by retaining only the terms with degree at most $d$ in the Hermite expansion of $A$, where recall that for ${\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n$, its degree is defined as $|{\boldsymbol \sigma}| = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma_i$.\\
	
	\noindent For convenience, in either case, define $A^{> d} := A - A^{\le d}$. Also, for vector valued functions $A$, we define $A^{\le d}$ as the function obtained by applying the above low-degree truncation on each coordinate.

nodes.name: Bonami-Beckner operator
nodes.statement: For any nu in [0,1], the Bonami-Beckner operator T_nu on a probability space (Z, mu) is given by its action on any f : Z to mathbb R, as follows, (T_nu f)(x) = E[f(Y) | X = x] where the conditional distribution of \ Y given X = x is nu delta_x + (1-nu) mu where delta_x is the delta measure on x. In other words, given X = x, we obtain Y by either setting it to x with probability nu or independently sampling from mu with probability (1-nu). For the product space (Z^n, mu^otimes n), we define the Bonami-Beckner operator T_nu as, T_nu = otimes_i=1^n T_nu^(i), where T_nu^(i) is the Bonami-Beckner operator on the i-th coordinate (Z, mu).

\label{lem:mossel_smoothing}
	Let $(\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu)$ be finite joint probability space, such that $\rho(\mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{Z}; \mu) = \rho$ for some $\rho \in [0,1]$. Let $P \in L^2(\mathcal{Z}^n, \mu_A^{\otimes n})$ and $Q \in L^2(\mathcal{Z}^n, \mu_B^{\otimes n})$ be multi-linear polynomials. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\nu$ be chosen sufficiently close to $1$ so that,
	\[\nu \ge (1-\varepsilon)^{\log \rho/(\log \varepsilon + \log \rho)}\]
	Then:
	\[\inabs{\inangle{P, Q}_{\mu^{\otimes n}} - \inangle{T_{\nu}P, T_{\nu}Q}_{\mu^{\otimes n}}} \le \varepsilon \cdot \sqrt{\mathsf{Var}[P] \mathsf{Var}[Q]}\]

	$$\nu ~\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}~ 1 - C \frac{(1-\rho)\varepsilon}{\log (1/\varepsilon)}$$

nodes.statement: Consider the Hermite expansions of P and Q. That is, \[ P(X) ~=~ sum_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n whatP(boldsymbol sigma) H_boldsymbol sigma(X) \ and \ Q(Y) ~=~ sum_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n whatQ(boldsymbol sigma) H_boldsymbol sigma(Y).\] Using properties of Hermite polynomials, namely, U_nu H_boldsymbol sigma = nu^|boldsymbol sigma| H_boldsymbol sigma, we get that, \[ U_nu P(X) ~=~ sum_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n nu^|boldsymbol sigma| whatP(boldsymbol sigma) H_boldsymbol sigma(X) \ and \ U_nu Q(Y) ~=~ sum_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n nu^|boldsymbol sigma| whatQ(boldsymbol sigma) H_boldsymbol sigma(Y).\] Note that our choice of nu gives us that, rho^d inparen1 - nu^2d le varepsilon for all d in mathbb N. Thus, we get that, &inabsinangleP, Q_G_rho^otimes n - inangleU_nuP, U_nuQ_G_rho^otimes n\\ &~=~ inabssumlimits_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n rho^|boldsymbol sigma| cdot whatP(boldsymbol sigma) whatQ(boldsymbol sigma) cdot inparen1 - nu^2|boldsymbol sigma|\\ &~le~ sumlimits_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n inabswhatP(boldsymbol sigma) whatQ(boldsymbol sigma) cdot rho^|boldsymbol sigma| inparen1 - nu^2|boldsymbol sigma|\\ &~le~ varepsilon cdot sumlimits_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n inabswhatP(boldsymbol sigma) whatQ(boldsymbol sigma) ldots (since, rho^d inparen1 - nu^2d le varepsilon for all d in mathbb N)\\ &~le~ varepsilon cdot sqrtVar[P] Var[Q] ldots (Cauchy-Schwarz inequality)

Consider the Hermite expansions of $P$ and $Q$. That is,
	\[ P(\mathbf{X}) ~=~ \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n} \what{P}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(\mathbf{X}) \qquad \ \mathrm{and} \ \qquad Q(\mathbf{Y}) ~=~ \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n} \what{Q}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(\mathbf{Y}).\]
	Using properties of Hermite polynomials, namely, $U_{\nu} H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}} = \nu^{|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|} H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}$, we get that,
	\[ U_\nu P(\mathbf{X}) ~=~ \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n} \nu^{|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|} \what{P}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(\mathbf{X}) \qquad \ \mathrm{and} \ \qquad U_\nu Q(\mathbf{Y}) ~=~ \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n} \nu^{|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|} \what{Q}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(\mathbf{Y}).\]
	Note that our choice of $\nu$ gives us that, $\rho^{d} \inparen{1 - \nu^{2d}} \le \varepsilon$ for all $d \in {\mathbb N}$. Thus, we get that,
	\begin{align*}
	&\inabs{\inangle{P, Q}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n}} - \inangle{U_{\nu}P, U_{\nu}Q}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n}}}\\
	&~=~ \inabs{\sum\limits_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n} \rho^{|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|} \cdot \what{P}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) \what{Q}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) \cdot \inparen{1 - \nu^{2|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|}}}\\
	&~\le~ \sum\limits_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n} \inabs{\what{P}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) \what{Q}({\boldsymbol \sigma})} \cdot \rho^{|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|} \inparen{1 - \nu^{2|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|}}\\
	
	&~\le~ \varepsilon \cdot \sum\limits_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n} \inabs{\what{P}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) \what{Q}({\boldsymbol \sigma})} \qquad \qquad \ldots (\text{since, } \rho^{d} \inparen{1 - \nu^{2d}} \le \varepsilon \text{ for all } d \in {\mathbb N})\\
	&~\le~ \varepsilon \cdot \sqrt{\mathsf{Var}[P] \mathsf{Var}[Q]} \qquad \qquad \ldots (\text{Cauchy-Schwarz inequality})
	\end{align*}
