nodes.statement: We prove the lemma for the case of correlated discrete hypercubes, i.e. (Z times Z, mu). The proof for the correlated Gaussian case follows similarly. We obtain A^(1) and B^(1) in two steps. In the first step we apply some suitable amount of noise to the functions such that the functions have decaying Fourier tails. In the second step, we truncate the Fourier coefficients corresponding to terms larger than degree d.\\ Noising step. In this step, we obtain intermediate functions overlineA : Z^n to mathbb R^k and overlineB : Z^n to mathbb R^k such that, item overlineA and overlineB have decaying Fourier tails. In particular, for any j in [k] : norm2overlineA_j^>d, norm2overlineB_j^>d le fracdelta2 sqrtk. item Var(overlineA_j) le Var(A_j) and Var(overlineB_j) le Var(B_j), for any j in [k]. item norm2R(overlineA) - overlineA le norm2R(A) - A and norm2R(overlineB) - overlineB le norm2R(B) - B. item For every i, j in [k] : inabsinangleoverlineA_i, overlineB_j_mu^otimes n - inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes n ~le~ fracdelta2 sqrtk. Firstly, note that we have Var[A_j], Var[B_j] le 1 for any j in [k]. Given parameter delta, we first choose varepsilon and nu in Lemma~, such that varepsilon = fracdelta2sqrtk and then nu = 1 - C frac(1-rho)varepsilonlog (1/varepsilon) as required. We choose d to be large enough such that nu^2d le fracdelta2sqrtk, that is, d = Oinparenfraclog (k/delta)log (1/nu) = Oinparenfracsqrtklog^2(k/delta)delta (1-rho). Let overlineA = T_nuA and overlineB = T_nuB. We get the above statements as follows, item norm2overlineA_j^> d ~=~ sumlimits_substackboldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_q^n \\ |boldsymbol sigma| > d nu^2|boldsymbol sigma| cdot whatA_j(boldsymbol sigma)^2 ~le~ nu^2d cdot Var(A_j) ~le~ fracdelta2sqrtk. Similarly, norm2overlineB_j^> d ~le~ fracdelta2sqrtk. item Var(overlineA_j) ~=~ sumlimits_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_q^n nu^2|boldsymbol sigma| cdot whatA_j(boldsymbol sigma)^2 ~le~ Var(A_j). Similarly, Var(overlineB) le Var(B). item Observe that norm2R(v) - v is the Euclidean distance of v in mathbb R^k from the simplex Delta_k, which is a convex body. Hence norm2R(v) - v^2 is convex function in v. Thus, we have that, & norm2R(overlineA) - overlineA^2\\ &~=~Elimits_bm x sim mu_A^otimes n norm2R(overlineA(bm x)) - overlineA(x)^2\\ &~=~ Elimits_bm x sim mu_A^otimes n norm2RinparenElimits_bm x' sim T_nu(bm x) A(bm x') - Elimits_bm x' sim T_nu(bm x) A(bm x')^2\\ &~le~ Elimits_bm x sim mu_A^otimes n Elimits_bm x' sim T_nu(bm x) norm2RinparenA(bm x') - A(bm x')^2 ldots(using convexity of norm2R(v) - v^2)\\ &~=~ Elimits_bm x' sim mu_A^otimes n norm2RinparenA(bm x') - A(bm x')^2\\ &~=~ norm2R(A) - A^2\;. Similar argument holds for overlineB. item For every i, j in [k], we simply have from Creflem:mossel_smoothing that inabsinangleoverlineA_i, overlineB_j_mu^otimes n - inangleA_i, B_j_mu^otimes n ~le~ varepsilon ~=~ fracdelta2 sqrtk. Low-degree truncation step. In this step, we obtain the final A^(1) and B^(1) such that, item A^(1) and B^(1) have degree at most d. item Var(A^(1)) le Var(overlineA) and Var(B^(1)) le Var(overlineB). item norm2R(A^(1)) - A^(1) le norm2R(overlineA) - overlineA + delta/2 and norm2R(B^(1)) - B^(1) le norm2R(overlineB) - overlineB + delta/2 item For every i, j in [k] : inabsinangleA^(1)_i, B^(1)_j_mu^otimes n - inangleoverlineA_i, overlineB_j_mu^otimes n ~le~ fracdelta2 sqrtk It is easy to see that combining statements 1-4 above, with statements 1-4 in the Noising step, we get all the desired conditions in Creflem:smoothing_main.\\ In this step, we let A^(1) = overlineA^le d and B^(1) = overlineB^le d (i.e. degree-d truncation on every coordinate j in [k]). We get the above statements as follows, item By definition of degree-d truncation, we have that A^(1) and B^(1) have degree at most d. item Var(A^(1)_j) ~=~ sumlimits_substackboldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_q^n \\ |boldsymbol sigma| le d nu^2|boldsymbol sigma| cdot whatA_j^(1)(boldsymbol sigma)^2 ~le~ Var(overlineA_j). Similarly, Var(B^(1)_j) ~le~ Var(overlineB_j). item We have that, norm2R(A^(1)) - A^(1) &~le~ norm2R(overlineA) - overlineA + norm2overlineA - A^(1) && (Creflem:close-to-simplex)\\ &~=~ norm2R(overlineA) - overlineA + norm2overlineA^> d\\ &~le~ norm2R(overlineA) - overlineA ~+~ sqrtk cdot fracdelta2sqrtk\\ &~le~ norm2R(overlineA) - overlineA ~+~ delta/2\;. Similarly for B^(1). item We have that norm2A^(1)_i - overlineA_ile fracdelta2sqrtk and norm2B^(1)_j - overlineB_j le fracdelta2sqrtk. Hence, using Creflem:close-strategies, we get that for every i, j in [k] \[inabsinangleA^(1)_i, B^(1)_j_mu^otimes n - inangleoverlineA_i, overlineB_j_mu^otimes n ~le~ fracdeltasqrtk\] This completes the proof of Creflem:smoothing_main for the case of correlated discrete hypercubes. The proof for the case of correlated Gaussians follows in almost the same way. The only change is that we use U_nu operator instead of T_nu operator, and use Creflem:gaussian_smoothing instead of Creflem:mossel_smoothing.
nodes.raw_latex:
We prove the lemma for the case of correlated discrete hypercubes, i.e. $(\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu)$. The proof for the correlated Gaussian case follows similarly.
	
	We obtain $A^{(1)}$ and $B^{(1)}$ in two steps. In the first step we apply some suitable amount of noise to the functions such that the functions have decaying Fourier tails. In the second step, we truncate the Fourier coefficients corresponding to terms larger than degree $d$.\\
	
	\noindent {\bf Noising step.} In this step, we obtain intermediate functions $\overline{A} : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $\overline{B} : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ such that,
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\overline{A}$ and $\overline{B}$ have decaying Fourier tails. In particular, for any $j \in [k]$ : $\norm{2}{\overline{A}_j^{>d}}, \norm{2}{\overline{B}_j^{>d}} \le \frac{\delta}{2 \sqrt{k}}$.
		\item $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{A}_j) \le \mathsf{Var}(A_j)$ and $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{B}_j) \le \mathsf{Var}(B_j)$, for any $j \in [k]$.
		\item $\norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{A}) - \overline{A}} \le \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(A) - A}$ and $\norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{B}) - \overline{B}} \le \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(B) - B}$.
		\item For every $i, j \in [k]$ : $\inabs{\inangle{\overline{A}_i, \overline{B}_j}_{\mu^{\otimes n}} - \inangle{A_i, B_j}_{\mu^{\otimes n}}} ~\le~ \frac{\delta}{2 \sqrt{k}}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	Firstly, note that we have $\mathsf{Var}[A_j], \mathsf{Var}[B_j] \le 1$ for any $j \in [k]$. Given parameter $\delta$, we first choose $\varepsilon$ and $\nu$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:mossel_smoothing}, such that $\varepsilon = \frac{\delta}{2\sqrt{k}}$ and then $\nu = 1 - C \frac{(1-\rho)\varepsilon}{\log (1/\varepsilon)}$ as required. We choose $d$ to be large enough such that $\nu^{2d} \le \frac{\delta}{2\sqrt{k}}$, that is, $d = O\inparen{\frac{\log (k/\delta)}{\log (1/\nu)}} = O\inparen{\frac{\sqrt{k}\log^2(k/\delta)}{\delta (1-\rho)}}$.
	
	Let $\overline{A} = T_{\nu}A$ and $\overline{B} = T_{\nu}B$. We get the above statements as follows,
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\norm{2}{\overline{A}_j^{> d}} ~=~ \sum\limits_{\substack{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_q^n \\ |{\boldsymbol \sigma}| > d}} \nu^{2|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|} \cdot \what{A_j}({\boldsymbol \sigma})^2 ~\le~ \nu^{2d} \cdot \mathsf{Var}(A_j) ~\le~ \frac{\delta}{2\sqrt{k}}$. Similarly, $\norm{2}{\overline{B}_j^{> d}} ~\le~ \frac{\delta}{2\sqrt{k}}$.
		
		\item $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{A}_j) ~=~ \sum\limits_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_q^n} \nu^{2|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|} \cdot \what{A_j}({\boldsymbol \sigma})^2 ~\le~ \mathsf{Var}(A_j)$. Similarly, $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{B}) \le \mathsf{Var}(B)$.
		
		\item Observe that $\norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(v) - v}$ is the Euclidean distance of $v \in {\mathbb R}^k$ from the simplex $\Delta_k$, which is a convex body. Hence $\norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(v) - v}^2$ is convex function in $v$. Thus, we have that,
		\begin{align*}
		& \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{A}) - \overline{A}}^2\\
		&~=~\mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm x} \sim \mu_A^{\otimes n}} \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{A}({\bm x})) - \overline{A}(x)}^2\\
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm x} \sim \mu_A^{\otimes n}} \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}\inparen{\mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm x}' \sim T_\nu({\bm x})} A({\bm x}')} - \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm x}' \sim T_\nu({\bm x})} A({\bm x}')}^2\\
		&~\le~ \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm x} \sim \mu_A^{\otimes n}} \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm x}' \sim T_\nu({\bm x})} \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}\inparen{A({\bm x}')} - A({\bm x}')}^2 \qquad \qquad \ldots(\text{using convexity of } \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(v) - v}^2)\\
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}\limits_{{\bm x}' \sim \mu_A^{\otimes n}} \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}\inparen{A({\bm x}')} - A({\bm x}')}^2\\
		&~=~ \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(A) - A}^2\;.
		\end{align*}
		Similar argument holds for $\overline{B}$.
		
		\item For every $i, j \in [k]$, we simply have from \Cref{lem:mossel_smoothing} that
		$\inabs{\inangle{\overline{A}_i, \overline{B}_j}_{\mu^{\otimes n}} - \inangle{A_i, B_j}_{\mu^{\otimes n}}} ~\le~ \varepsilon ~=~ \frac{\delta}{2 \sqrt{k}}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\noindent {\bf Low-degree truncation step.} In this step, we obtain the final $A^{(1)}$ and $B^{(1)}$ such that,
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $A^{(1)}$ and $B^{(1)}$ have degree at most $d$.
		\item $\mathsf{Var}(A^{(1)}) \le \mathsf{Var}(\overline{A})$ and $\mathsf{Var}(B^{(1)}) \le \mathsf{Var}(\overline{B})$.
		\item $\norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(A^{(1)}) - A^{(1)}} \le \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{A}) - \overline{A}} + \delta/2$ and $\norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(B^{(1)}) - B^{(1)}} \le \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{B}) - \overline{B}} + \delta/2$
		\item For every $i, j \in [k]$ : $\inabs{\inangle{A^{(1)}_i, B^{(1)}_j}_{\mu^{\otimes n}} - \inangle{\overline{A}_i, \overline{B}_j}_{\mu^{\otimes n}}} ~\le~ \frac{\delta}{2 \sqrt{k}}$
	\end{enumerate}
	It is easy to see that combining statements 1-4 above, with statements 1-4 in the Noising step, we get all the desired conditions in \Cref{lem:smoothing_main}.\\
	
	\noindent In this step, we let $A^{(1)} = \overline{A}^{\le d}$ and $B^{(1)} = \overline{B}^{\le d}$ (i.e. degree-$d$ truncation on every coordinate $j \in [k]$). We get the above statements as follows,
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item By definition of degree-$d$ truncation, we have that $A^{(1)}$ and $B^{(1)}$ have degree at most $d$.
		\item $\mathsf{Var}(A^{(1)}_j) ~=~ \sum\limits_{\substack{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_q^n \\ |{\boldsymbol \sigma}| \le d}} \nu^{2|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|} \cdot \what{A}_j^{(1)}({\boldsymbol \sigma})^2 ~\le~ \mathsf{Var}(\overline{A}_j)$. Similarly, $\mathsf{Var}(B^{(1)}_j) ~\le~ \mathsf{Var}(\overline{B}_j)$.
		\item We have that,
		\begin{align*}
		\norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(A^{(1)}) - A^{(1)}}
		&~\le~ \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{A}) - \overline{A}} + \norm{2}{\overline{A} - A^{(1)}} && \text{(\Cref{lem:close-to-simplex})}\\
		&~=~ \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{A}) - \overline{A}} + \norm{2}{\overline{A}^{> d}}\\
		&~\le~ \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{A}) - \overline{A}} ~+~ \sqrt{k} \cdot \frac{\delta}{2\sqrt{k}}\\
		&~\le~ \norm{2}{\mathcal{R}(\overline{A}) - \overline{A}} ~+~ \delta/2\;.
		\end{align*}
		Similarly for $B^{(1)}$.
		\item We have that $\norm{2}{A^{(1)}_i - \overline{A}_i}\le \frac{\delta}{2\sqrt{k}}$ and $\norm{2}{B^{(1)}_j - \overline{B}_j} \le \frac{\delta}{2\sqrt{k}}$. Hence, using \Cref{lem:close-strategies}, we get that for every $i, j \in [k]$
		\[\inabs{\inangle{A^{(1)}_i, B^{(1)}_j}_{\mu^{\otimes n}} - \inangle{\overline{A}_i, \overline{B}_j}_{\mu^{\otimes n}}} ~\le~ \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{k}}\]
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\noindent This completes the proof of \Cref{lem:smoothing_main} for the case of correlated discrete hypercubes. The proof for the case of correlated Gaussians follows in almost the same way. The only change is that we use $U_\nu$ operator instead of $T_\nu$ operator, and use \Cref{lem:gaussian_smoothing} instead of \Cref{lem:mossel_smoothing}.

nodes.name: Multilinear truncation
nodes.statement: Suppose A in L^2(mathbb R^n, gamma_n) is given by the Hermite expansion A(x) = sumlimits_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^n whatA_boldsymbol sigma H_boldsymbol sigma(x). The multilinear truncation of A is defined as the function A^ml in L^2(mathbb R^n, gamma_n) given by \[A^ml(x) ~:=~ sum_boldsymbol sigma in set0,1^n whatA_boldsymbol sigma H_boldsymbol sigma(x).\] That is, A^ml is obtained by retaining only the multilinear terms in the Hermite expansion of A.\\ For convenience, also define A^nml := A - A^ml. Also, for vector valued functions A, we define A^ml as the function obtained by applying the above multilinear truncation on each coordinate.

\label{def:ml_truncation}
	Suppose $A \in L^2({\mathbb R}^n, \gamma_n)$ is given by the Hermite expansion $A(x) = \sum\limits_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^n} \what{A}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}} H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(x)$. The {\em multilinear truncation} of $A$ is defined as the function $A^{\mathrm{ml}} \in L^2({\mathbb R}^n, \gamma_n)$ given by
	\[A^{\mathrm{ml}}(x) ~:=~ \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in \set{0,1}^n} \what{A}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}} H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(x).\]
	That is, $A^{\mathrm{ml}}$ is obtained by retaining only the multilinear terms in the Hermite expansion of $A$.\\
	For convenience, also define $A^{\mathrm{nml}} := A - A^{\mathrm{ml}}$. Also, for vector valued functions $A$, we define $A^{\mathrm{ml}}$ as the function obtained by applying the above multilinear truncation on each coordinate.

\label{lem:non-ml-to-ml}
	Given parameters $\rho \in [0,1]$, $\delta>0$ and $d \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}$, there exists $t = t(d, \delta)$ such that the following holds:
	
	Let $A, B \in L^2({\mathbb R}^n, \gamma_n)$ be degree-$d$ polynomials, such that $\norm{2}{A}, \norm{2}{B} \le 1$. Define polynomials $\overline{A}, \overline{B} \in L^2({\mathbb R}^{nt}, \gamma_{nt})$ over variables $\overline{\mathbf{X}} := \setdef{X^{(i)}_j}{(i,j) \in [n] \times [t]}$ and $\overline{\mathbf{Y}} := \setdef{Y^{(i)}_j}{(i,j) \in [n] \times [t]}$ respectively, as,
	\[ \overline{A}\inparen{\overline{\mathbf{X}}} := A(X^{(1)}, \ldots, X^{(n)}) \qquad \ \mathrm{and} \ \qquad \overline{B}\inparen{\overline{\mathbf{Y}}} := B(Y^{(1)}, \ldots, Y^{(n)})
	\]
	where $X^{(i)} = \inparen{X^{(i)}_1 + \cdots + X^{(i)}_t}/\sqrt{t}$ and $Y^{(i)} = \inparen{Y^{(i)}_1 + \cdots + Y^{(i)}_t}/\sqrt{t}$. Note that, intuitively this doesn't change the ``structure'' of $A$ and $B$. In particular, it is easy to see that,
	\[\inangle{\overline{A}, \overline{B}}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes nt}} \ = \ \inangle{A, B}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n}} \quad \ \mathrm{and} \ \quad \norm{2}{\overline{A}} = \norm{2}{A} \quad \ \mathrm{and} \ \quad \norm{2}{\overline{B}} = \norm{2}{B}\]
	
	\noindent Next, let $\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}, \overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}} \in L^2({\mathbb R}^{nt}, \gamma_{nt})$ be the multilinear truncations of $\overline{A}$ and $\overline{B}$ respectively. Then the following hold,
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}$ and $\overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}$ are multilinear with degree $d$.
		\item $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}) \le \mathsf{Var}(A) \le 1$ and $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}) \le \mathsf{Var}(B) \le 1$.
		\item $\norm{2}{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}} - \overline{A}}, \norm{2}{\overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}} - \overline{B}} ~\le~ \delta/2$.
		\item For all $(i,j) \in [n] \times [t]$, it holds that $\mathrm{Inf}_{X^{(i)}_j}\inparen{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}} \le \delta$ and $\mathrm{Inf}_{Y^{(i)}_j}\inparen{\overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}} \le \delta$.
		\item $\inabs{\inangle{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}, \overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes nt}} - \inangle{A, B}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n}}} ~\le~ \delta$.
	\end{enumerate}

Before we prove the theorem, we will first understand the effect of the transformation from $X$ to $\overline{X}$ for a single Hermite polynomial. Instantiating $\beta_i$'s in \Cref{fact:multinomial_hermite} with $1/\sqrt{t}$, we get that,
	\[ H_d\inparen{\frac{X_1 + \cdots + X_t}{\sqrt{t}}} \ = \ \sum_{\substack{d_1, \ldots, d_t \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0} \\ d_1 + \cdots + d_t = d}} \sqrt{\frac{d!}{d_1! \cdots d_t!}} \cdot \frac{\prod_{i=1}^{t} H_{d_i}(X_i)}{t^{d/2}}\;.\]
	
	
	We will split the terms into multilinear and non-multilinear terms, writing the above as $H_d^{\mathrm{ml}} + H_d^{\mathrm{nml}}$. Note that there are at most $O(\frac{d^2 t^{d-1}}{d!})$ non-multilinear terms (for $t \gg d^2$). Also, note that each coefficient $\frac{1}{t^{d/2}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{d!}{d_1! \cdots d_t!}}$ is at most $\sqrt{\frac{d!}{t^d}}$. Thus, we can bound $\norm{2}{H_d^{\mathrm{nml}}}$ as follows,
	\begin{equation}
	\norm{2}{H^{\mathrm{nml}}}^2 \quad = \quad \sum_{\substack{d_1, \ldots, d_t \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0} \\ d_1 + \cdots + d_t = d \\ \exists i\,\ d_i \ge 2}} \inparen{\frac{1}{t^{d/2}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{d!}{d_1! \cdots d_t!}}}^2 \quad \le \quad O\inparen{\frac{d^2 t^{d-1}}{d!}} \cdot \frac{d!}{t^d} \quad \le \quad O\inparen{\frac{d^2}{t}} \label{eqn:nml_small}
	\end{equation}
	
	\noindent More generally, if we consider a term $\overline{H}_{\boldsymbol \sigma}\inparen{\overline{\mathbf{X}}} = H_{\sigma_1}(X^{(1)}) \cdot H_{\sigma_2}(X^{(2)}) \cdots H_{\sigma_N}(X^{(N)})$, where each $X^{(i)} = \inparen{X^{(i)}_1 + \cdots + X^{(i)}_t}/\sqrt{t}$. Let's write $\overline{H}_{\boldsymbol \sigma}\inparen{\overline{\mathbf{X}}} = \overline{H}_{\boldsymbol \sigma}^{\mathrm{ml}}\inparen{\overline{\mathbf{X}}} + \overline{H}_{\boldsymbol \sigma}^{\mathrm{nml}}\inparen{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}$, that is, separating out the multilinear and non-multilinear terms. Similarly, for any $i$, let $H_{\sigma_i}(X^{(i)}) = H_{\sigma_i}^{\mathrm{ml}}(X^{(i)}) + H_{\sigma_i}^{\mathrm{nml}}(X^{(i)})$. 
	We wish to bound $\norm{2}{\overline{H}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}^{\mathrm{nml}}}$, which can be done as follows,
	\begin{align}
	\norm{2}{\overline{H}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}^{\mathrm{nml}}}^2 &~=~ \norm{2}{\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n}(H_{\sigma_i}^{\mathrm{ml}} + H_{\sigma_i}^{\mathrm{nml}}) - \prod\limits_{i=1}^n H_{\sigma_i}^{\mathrm{ml}}}^2 \nonumber\\
	&~\le~ \prod_{i=1}^n \inparen{1+O\inparen{\frac{\sigma_i^2}{t}}} - 1 && \text{(from \Cref{eqn:nml_small})} \nonumber\\
	&~\le~ O\inparen{\frac{|{\boldsymbol \sigma}|^2}{t}} && \text{(since, $t \gg |{\boldsymbol \sigma}|^2$)} \nonumber\\
	\text{Thus, }\quad \norm{2}{\overline{H}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}^{\mathrm{nml}}}^2 &~<~ \delta^2/4. && (\text{for } t = \Theta(d^2/\delta^2))\label{eqn:global_nml_small}
	\end{align}
	
	\noindent We are now ready to prove the parts of our \Cref{lem:non-ml-to-ml}.
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item It holds by definition that $\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}$ and $\overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}$ are multilinear. Also, note that the transformation from $A$ to $\overline{A}$ and finally to $\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}$ does not increase the degree. So both  $\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}$ and $\overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}$ have degree at most $d$.
		
		\item It is easy to see that $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{A}) = \mathsf{Var}(A)$. Since $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}})$ is obtained by truncating certain Hermite coefficients of $\overline{A}$, it immediately follows that $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}) \le \mathsf{Var}(\overline{A}) = \mathsf{Var}(A) \le 1$. Similarly, $\mathsf{Var}(\overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}) \le \mathsf{Var}(B) \le 1$.
		
		\item Recall that $\overline{A}^{\mathrm{nml}} = \overline{A} - \overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}$. We wish to bound $\norm{2}{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{nml}}}^2 \le \delta^2/4$. Consider the Hermite expansion of $A$, namely $A(\mathbf{X}) = \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^N} \what{A}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) \cdot H_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(\mathbf{X})$. Note that, $\overline{A}^{\mathrm{nml}}\inparen{\overline{\mathbf{X}}} = \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^N} \what{A}({\boldsymbol \sigma}) \cdot \overline{H}^{\mathrm{nml}}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}\inparen{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}$, where recall that $\overline{H}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}^{\mathrm{nml}}$ is the non-multilinear part of $\overline{H}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}\inparen{\overline{\mathbf{X}}} = H_{\sigma_1}(X^{(1)}) \cdot H_{\sigma_2}(X^{(2)}) \cdots H_{\sigma_n}(X^{(N)})$, where each $X^{(i)} = \inparen{X^{(i)}_1 + \cdots + X^{(i)}_t}/\sqrt{t}$.
		
		From Equation~\ref{eqn:global_nml_small}, we have that for any ${\boldsymbol \sigma} \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}^N$, it holds that $\norm{2}{\overline{H}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}^{\mathrm{nml}}\inparen{\overline{X}}}^2 < \delta^2/4$. And hence we get that,
		\[ \norm{2}{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{nml}}}^2 ~=~ \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}} \what{A}({\boldsymbol \sigma})^2 \cdot \norm{2}{\overline{H}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}^{\mathrm{nml}}}^2 ~\le~ \sum_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}} \what{A}({\boldsymbol \sigma})^2 \cdot (\delta^2/4) ~=~ (\delta^2/4) \norm{2}{A}^2 ~\le~ (\delta^2/4). \]
		Note that, here we use that $\overline{H}_{{\boldsymbol \sigma}}(\overline{\mathbf{X}})$ are mutually orthogonal for different ${\boldsymbol \sigma}$. Similarly, we can also get that $\norm{2}{\overline{B}^{\mathrm{nml}}}^2 \le \delta^2/4$.
		
		\item We prove that $\mathrm{Inf}_{X^{(i)}_j}\inparen{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}} ~\le~ d/t ~<~ \delta^2/d ~<~ \delta$. The case $\mathrm{Inf}_{Y^{(i)}_j}\inparen{\overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}}$ will follow similarly.
		
		For simplicity, let's first consider the case of a univariate polynomial $P \in L^2({\mathbb R}, \gamma_1)$ of degree-$d$, such that $\norm{2}{P} \le 1$. We will show that for the function $\overline{P}(X_1, \cdots, X_t) := P \inparen{\frac{X_1 + \cdots + X_t}{\sqrt{t}}}$, it holds that $\mathrm{Inf}_{X_i}\inparen{\overline{P}^{\mathrm{ml}}} \le \mathsf{Var}(P)\cdot (d/t)$. This follows from a few simple observations:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item By symmetry, $\mathrm{Inf}_{X_i}\inparen{\overline{P}^{\mathrm{ml}}}$ is the same for all $i$.
			\item For degree-$d$ multilinear polynomials, $\sum_{i \in [t]} \mathrm{Inf}_{X_i}\inparen{\overline{P}^{\mathrm{ml}}} \le d \mathsf{Var}\inparen{\overline{P}^{\mathrm{ml}}}$. 
			\item $\mathsf{Var}\inparen{\overline{P}^{\mathrm{ml}}} \le \mathsf{Var}\inparen{\overline{P}} = \mathsf{Var}(P)$
		\end{enumerate}
		Thus, combining the above, we get that $\mathrm{Inf}_{X_i}\inparen{\overline{P}^{\mathrm{ml}}} \le \mathsf{Var}(P)\cdot (d/t)$.\\
		
		In the more general case $n$-variate case, we observe that,
		\begin{align*}
		\mathrm{Inf}_{X^{(i)}_j}\inparen{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}} &~=~ \mathbb{E}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}} \setminus \set{X^{(i)}_j}} \ \mathsf{Var}_{X^{(i)}_j} \inparen{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}_{\overline{X} \setminus \set{X^{(i)}_j}} \inparen{X^{(i)}_j}}\\
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}^{(-i)}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}^{(i)}_{-j}} \mathsf{Var}_{X^{(i)}_j} \inparen{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}_{\overline{X} \setminus \set{X^{(i)}_j}} \inparen{X^{(i)}_j}} && \text{(for simplicity, $\mathbf{X}^{(-i)} := \overline{\mathbf{X}} \setminus \setdef{X^{(i)}_j}{j \in [t]}$)}\\
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}^{(-i)}} \mathrm{Inf}_{X^{(i)}_j} \inparen{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}_{X^{(-i)}}(X^{(i)})}\\
		&~=~ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}^{(-i)}} \mathsf{Var}\inparen{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}_{X^{(-i)}}} \cdot (d/t)\\
		&~\le~ (d/t) \cdot \mathrm{Inf}_i(A)\\
		&~\le~ d/t\\
		&~<~ \delta.
		\end{align*}
		where, in last two inequalities, we use that $\mathrm{Inf}_i(A) \le \mathsf{Var}(A) \le 1$ and that $t = \Theta(d^2/\delta^2)$.
		
		\item Note that we already have,
		\[ \inangle{\overline{A}, \overline{B}}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes nt}} \ = \ \inangle{A, B}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n}}\;. \]
		And combining Part 3 and \Cref{lem:close-strategies}, we immediately get that
		\[\inabs{\inangle{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}, \overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes nt}} - \inangle{\overline{A}, \overline{B}}_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes nt}}} ~\le~ \delta\] 
		where we use that $\norm{2}{\overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}} \le \norm{2}{\overline{B}} \le 1$ and $\norm{2}{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}} \le \norm{2}{\overline{A}} \le 1$.
	\end{enumerate}

Consider the Hermite expansion of A, namely A(X) = sum_boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^N whatA(boldsymbol sigma) cdot H_boldsymbol sigma(X). From Equation~, we have that for any boldsymbol sigma in mathbb Z_ge 0^N, it holds that norm2overlineH_boldsymbol sigma^nmlinparenoverlineX^2 < delta^2/4. And hence we get that, \[ norm2overlineA^nml^2 ~=~ sum_boldsymbol sigma whatA(boldsymbol sigma)^2 cdot norm2overlineH_boldsymbol sigma^nml^2 ~le~ sum_boldsymbol sigma whatA(boldsymbol sigma)^2 cdot (delta^2/4) ~=~ (delta^2/4) norm2A^2 ~le~ (delta^2/4). \] Note that, here we use that overlineH_boldsymbol sigma(overlineX) are mutually orthogonal for different boldsymbol sigma. Similarly, we can also get that norm2overlineB^nml^2 le delta^2/4. item We prove that Inf_X^(i)_jinparenoverlineA^ml ~le~ d/t ~<~ delta^2/d ~<~ delta. The case Inf_Y^(i)_jinparenoverlineB^ml will follow similarly. For simplicity, let's first consider the case of a univariate polynomial P in L^2(mathbb R, gamma_1) of degree-d, such that norm2P le 1. We will show that for the function overlineP(X_1, cdots, X_t) := P inparenfracX_1 + cdots + X_tsqrtt, it holds that Inf_X_iinparenoverlineP^ml le Var(P)cdot (d/t). nodes.name: Proof of \Cref{lem:multilin_main}
nodes.statement: We apply the transformation in Creflem:non-ml-to-ml, with parameter delta being delta/sqrtk, to each of the k-coordinates of A : mathbb R^n to mathbb R^k and B : mathbb R^n to mathbb R^k to get function A^(1) : mathbb R^nt to mathbb R^k and B^(1) : mathbb R^n to mathbb R^k. Namely, for any j in [k], we set A^(1)_j(overlineX) = overlineA^ml_j(overlineX) and B^(1)_j(overlineY) = overlineB^ml_j(overlineY)as described in Creflem:non-ml-to-ml. It is easy to see that parts 1, 2, 4, 5 follow immediately from the conditions satisfied in Creflem:non-ml-to-ml. For part 3, we note that we have that norm2overlineA^ml_j - overlineA_j le delta/sqrtk for every j in [k]. Thus, combining these for all j in [k], we get that norm2overlineA^ml - overlineA le delta. Now, using Creflem:close-to-simplex, we immediately get that, \[norm2R(overlineA^ml) - overlineA^ml le norm2R(overlineA) - overlineA + delta\;.\] Finally, we observe that norm2R(overlineA) - overlineA = norm2R(A) - A, to conclude that \[norm2R(A^(1)) - A^(1) le norm2R(A) - A + delta\;.\] Similarly, norm2R(B^(1)) - B^(1) le norm2R(B) - B + delta. This concludes the proof.

Namely, for any $j \in [k]$, we set $A^{(1)}_j(\overline{\mathbf{X}}) = \overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}_j(\overline{\mathbf{X}})$ and $B^{(1)}_j(\overline{\mathbf{Y}}) = \overline{B}^{\mathrm{ml}}_j(\overline{\mathbf{Y}})$as described in \Cref{lem:non-ml-to-ml}.
	
	It is easy to see that parts 1, 2, 4, 5 follow immediately from the conditions satisfied in \Cref{lem:non-ml-to-ml}. For part 3, we note that we have that $
orm{2}{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}}_j - \overline{A}_j} \le \delta/\sqrt{k}$ for every $j \in [k]$. Thus, combining these for all $j \in [k]$, we get that $
orm{2}{\overline{A}^{\mathrm{ml}} - \overline{A}} \le \delta$. Now, using \Cref{lem:close-to-simplex}, we immediately get that,
	\[

orm{2}{\mathcal{R}(A) - A}$, to conclude that 
	\[
orm{2}{\mathcal{R}(A^{(1)}) - A^{(1)}} \le 
orm{2}{\mathcal{R}(A) - A} + \delta\;.\]
	Similarly, $
orm{2}{\mathcal{R}(B^{(1)}) - B^{(1)}} \le 
orm{2}{\mathcal{R}(B) - B} + \delta$. This concludes the proof.

nodes.statement: Let (Z times Z, mu) be a joint probability space. Let k, d in mathbb N and tau > 0 be any given constant parameters. There exists h stackreldef= h((Z times Z, mu), k, d, tau) such that the following holds: For all degree-d polynomials P : Z^n to mathbb R^k and Q : Z^n to mathbb R^k such that, Var[P_j] le 1 and Var[Q_j] le 1 for all j in [k], there exists a subset of indices H subseteq [n] with |H| le h such that with probability at least (1-tau) over the assignment (xi_A, xi_B) sim mu^otimes h, the following holds for any j in [k] (where we denote T = [n] setminus H), item the restriction P_j^xi_A(x_T) is such that for all i in T, it holds that Inf_i(P_j^xi_A(x_T)) le tau, item the restriction Q_j^xi_B(y_T) is such that for all i in T, it holds that Inf_i(Q_j^xi_B(y_T)) le tau. nodes.name: Regularity Lemma for degree-$d$ functions
nodes.statement: Let (Z, mu_A) be a probability space. Let d in mathbb N and tau > 0 be any given constant parameters. There exists h stackreldef= h((Z, mu_A), d, tau) such that the following holds: For all degree-d multilinear polynomials P in L^2(Z^n, mu_A^otimes n) with Var[P] le 1, there exists a subset of indices H_0 subseteq [n] with |H_0| le h, such that for any superset H supseteq H_0, the restrictions of P obtained by evaluating the coordinates in H according to distribution mu_A, satisfies the following (where we denote T = [n] setminus H): Prlimits_xi sim mu_A^otimes |H| insquareforall i in T : Inf_i(P^xi(x_T)) le tau ge 1-tau In other words, with probability at least 1-tau over the random restriction xi sim mu_A^otimes |H|, the restricted function P^xi(x_T) is such that Inf_i(P^xi(x_T)) le tau for all i in T. In particular, one may take h = fracdtau cdot inparenfracC_4(alpha)alpha log fracC_4(alpha)alpha cdot d cdot tau^O(d) which is a constant that depends on d, tau and alpha stackreldef= alpha(mu_A).

\label{lem:single_reg_lem}
	Let $(\mathcal{Z}, \mu_A)$ be a probability space. Let $d \in {\mathbb N}$ and $\tau > 0$ be any given constant parameters. There exists $h \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} h((\mathcal{Z}, \mu_A), d, \tau)$ such that the following holds:
	
	For all degree-$d$ multilinear polynomials $P \in L^2(\mathcal{Z}^n, \mu_{A}^{\otimes n})$ with $\mathsf{Var}[P] \le 1$, there exists a subset of indices $H_0 \subseteq [n]$ with $|H_0| \le h$, such that for any superset $H \supseteq H_0$, the restrictions of $P$ obtained by evaluating the coordinates in $H$ according to distribution $\mu_A$, satisfies the following (where we denote $T = [n] \setminus H$):
	$$\Pr\limits_{\xi \sim \mu_A^{\otimes |H|}} \insquare{\forall i \in T : \mathrm{Inf}_i(P^{\xi}(x_T)) \le \tau} \ge 1-\tau$$
	In other words, with probability at least $1-\tau$ over the random restriction $\xi \sim \mu_{A}^{\otimes |H|}$, the restricted function $P^{\xi}(x_T)$ is such that $\mathrm{Inf}_i(P^{\xi}(x_T)) \le \tau$ for all $i \in T$.
	
	\noindent In particular, one may take $h = \frac{d}{\tau} \cdot \inparen{\frac{C_4(\alpha)}{\alpha} \log \frac{C_4(\alpha)}{\alpha \cdot d \cdot \tau}}^{O(d)}$ which is a constant that depends on $d$, $\tau$ and $\alpha \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} \alpha(\mu_A)$.

nodes.name: Proof of \Cref{lem:joint_regularity}
nodes.statement: We invoke the Regularity Lemma for individual degree-d polynomials Creflem:single_reg_lem, namely P_j's and Q_j's and then applying a union bound. In particular, given our parameters d and tau, we invoke Creflem:single_reg_lem with parameters d and tau/2k for each P_j and Q_j. Suppose we get the set H_A^(j) (resp. H_B^(j)) when applying the regularity lemma on P_j (resp. Q_j). We let H = bigcup_j in [k] inparenH_A^(j) cup H_B^(j). Note that, |H| le 2k cdot frac2dktau cdot inparenfracC_4(alpha)alpha log fracC_4(alpha) cdot kalpha cdot d cdot tau^O(d). Creflem:single_reg_lem gives us that for this H, it holds for any P_j and Q_j that, \[ Prlimits_xi_A sim mu_A^otimes |H| insquareforall i in T : Inf_iinparenP_j^xi_A(x_T) le tau/2k ge 1-(tau/2k) \] \[ Prlimits_xi_B sim mu_B^otimes |H| insquareforall i in T : Inf_iinparenQ_j^xi_B(y_T) le tau/2k ge 1-(tau/2k) \] Taking a union bound over 2k such statements in total, we get the conclusion we desire.

nodes.statement: Let (Z times Z, mu) be a finite joint probability space, such that |Z| = q and alpha := alpha(mu) > 0 is the minimum probability of any atom in mu. Given parameters k, d in mathbb N and delta > 0, there exists tau = tau((Z times Z, mu), k, d, delta) such that the following holds: Let A : Z^n to mathbb R^k and B : Z^n to mathbb R^k be degree-d multilinear polynomials, such that, Var(A_j), Var(B_j) le 1 and Inf_ell(A_j), Inf_ell(B_j) le tau for all ell in [n] and j in [k]. Then, there exist degree-d multilinear polynomials wtildeA : mathbb R^n cdot (q-1) to mathbb R^k and wtildeB : mathbb R^n cdot (q-1) to mathbb R^k, such that, for all i, j in [k], it holds that, inabsinangleR_i(wtildeA), R_j(wtildeB)_G_rho^otimes n (q-1) ~-~ inangleR_i(A), R_j(B)_mu^otimes n le delta\;, where rho = rho(Z, Z; mu) is the maximal correlation of mu. In particular, one may take tau = Oinparenfracdelta^1.5 cdot alpha^d/22^O(d) cdot 2^O(k). Additionally, the theorem also works in reverse, namely, given degree-d multilinear polynomials wtildeA : mathbb R^n to mathbb R^k and wtildeB : mathbb R^n to mathbb R^k, such that Var(wtildeA_j), Var(wtildeB_j) le 1 and Inf_ell(wtildeA_j), Inf_ell(wtildeB_j) le tau for all ell in [n] and j in [k], there exist A : Z^n to mathbb R^k and B : Z^n to mathbb R^k, such that Crefeqn:our_invariance holds.

nodes.name: Invariance Principle (cf. \cite{isaksson2012maximally})
nodes.statement: Let (Omega^n, mu^otimes n) be a finite probability space, such that alpha > 0 is the minimum probability of any atom in mu. Let F = (F_1, ldots, F_n) be an independent sequence of orthonormal ensembles such that F_ell is a basis for functions Omega to mathbb R, for any ell in [n]. Let P be a K-dimensional multilinear polynomial such that for every j in [K], it holds that Var(P_j) le 1, deg(P_j) le d and Inf_i (P_j) le tau for every i in [n]. Finally, let Psi: mathbb R^K to mathbb R be Lipschitz continuous with Lipschitz constant L. Then, \[ inabsE_F Psi(P(F)) - E_G Psi(P(G)) ~le~ D_K cdot L cdot inparend (8/sqrtalpha)^d sqrttau^1/3\;,\] where G is an independent sequence of Gaussian ensembles with same covariance structure as F and D_K = 2^O(K).footnoteNote that the lemma stated in does not state the explicit bound of D_K = 2^O(K). However, it is possible to infer this bound from their proof.

Let P be a K-dimensional multilinear polynomial such that for every j in [K], it holds that Var(P_j) le 1, deg(P_j) le d and Inf_i (P_j) le tau for every i in [n].
Finally, let Psi: mathbb R^K to mathbb R be Lipschitz continuous with Lipschitz constant L.

However, it is possible to infer this bound from their proof.

nodes.name: Proof of \Cref{lem:our_invariance}
nodes.statement: We will apply Creflem:invariance on the space (Omega^n, mu^otimes n) = (Z^n times Z^n, mu^otimes n). We consider the independent sequence of orthonormal ensembles F given by F_ell = setdefX^(ell)_i(x) Y^(ell)_j(y)i, j in set0, ldots, q-1 for any ell in [n] (where, recall that |Z| = q). Although as defined F_ell has q^2 elements, the polynomials we consider will only depend on the subset of characters setdefX^(ell)_1, ldots, X^(ell)_q-1, Y^(ell)_1, ldots, Y^(ell)_q-1ell in [n]. Also, observe that we can choose the characters setX^(ell)_i and setY^(ell)_i such that inangleX^(ell)_i, Y^(ell)_j_mu = rho_i cdot 1_seti=j, where rho_1 = rho(Z, Z; mu) is the maximal correlation, and rho_i le rho for all 1 le i le q-1. Given degree-d multilinear polynomials A : Z^n to mathbb R^k and B : Z^n to mathbb R^k, we consider the polynomial P : Z times Z to mathbb R^2k given by P = (P_1, ldots, P_2k), where for j le k, we take P_j(bm x, bm y) = A_j(bm x) and for j > k, we take P_j(bm x, bm y) = B_j-k(bm y). In other words, P is a concatenation of A and B. It is clear that P is also a degree-d multilinear polynomial in F. Also, since A and B are such that Var(A_j), Var(B_j) le 1 and Inf_ell(A_j), Inf_ell(B_j) le tau for all ell in [n] and j in [k], we have that for all j in [2k], it holds that, Var(P_j) le 1 and Inf_ell(P_j) le tau. Thus, P satisfies all the conditions needed to prove Creflem:invariance. We will use the test function Psi : mathbb R^2k to mathbb R, given by Psi(bm u,bm v) := R_i(bm u) cdot R_j(bm v), for any given i, j in [k]. It is easy to show that R(cdot) is a contraction map (since it is rounding to Delta_k which is a convex body), and hence any coordinate R_i(cdot) has Lipschitz constant of at most 1. This gives us that our test function Psi(bm u, bm v) = R_i(bm u) cdot R_j(bm v) also has a Lipschitz constant of at most 1. We can interpret the invariance principle, as substituting setdefX^(ell)_1, ldots, X^(ell)_q-1, Y^(ell)_1, ldots, Y^(ell)_q-1ell in [n] by correlated multivariate Gaussians (g^(ell), h^(ell)) = (g^(ell)_1, cdots, g^(ell)_q-1, h^(ell)_1, ldots, h^(ell)_q-1), such that E g^(ell)_i h^(ell)_j = rho_i cdot 1_seti=j and E g^(ell)_i g^(ell)_j = E h^(ell)_i h^(ell)_j = 1_seti=j. Thus the invariance principle is taking P : Z^n times Z^n to mathbb R^2k and producing P' : mathbb R^(q-1)n times mathbb R^(q-1)n to mathbb R^2k. Note that the first k coordinates of P are polynomials over the subset setdefX^(ell)_1, ldots, X^(ell)_q-1ell in [n] and the latter k coordinates are polynomials over setdefY^(ell)_1, ldots, Y^(ell)_q-1ell in [n]. Hence we can interpret the first k coordinates as A' : mathbb R^(q-1)n to mathbb R^k and latter k coordinates as B' : mathbb R^(q-1)n to mathbb R^k, and Creflem:invariance gives us that, \[ inabsinangleR_i(A'), R_j(B')_G^otimes n - inangleR_i(A), R_j(B)_mu^otimes n ~le~ 2^O(k) cdot inparend (8/sqrtalpha)^d sqrttau^1/3 ~le~ delta \] for a choice of tau le Oinparenfracdelta^1.5 cdot alpha^d/22^O(d) cdot 2^O(k). We are still not done though! We want wtildeA and wtildeB which act on coorrelated inputs sampled from G_rho^otimes (q-1)n, that is, (g^(ell), h^(ell)) = (g^(ell)_1, cdots, g^(ell)_q-1, h^(ell)_1, ldots, h^(ell)_q-1), such that E g^(ell)_i h^(ell)_j = rho cdot 1_seti=j and E g^(ell)_i g^(ell)_j = E h^(ell)_i h^(ell)_j = 1_seti=j. However the correlation pattern obtained in G is not exactly this. But note that each rho_i le rho. Thus, given (g^(ell)_i, h^(ell)_i) with correlation rho, we can simply apply U_rho_i/rho operator on h^(ell)_i to bring down the correlation from rho to rho_i. Applying this appropriate operation for every ell in [n] and i in [q], we get our desired wtildeA : mathbb R^n cdot (q-1) to mathbb R^k and wtildeB : mathbb R^n cdot (q-1) to mathbb R^k. The reverse part of the theorem follows similarly as well. Here, we get polynomials A and B, that depend only on setX^(ell)_1 and setY^(ell)_1 respectively.

We will apply \Cref{lem:invariance} on the space $(\Omega^n, \mu^{\otimes n}) = (\mathcal{Z}^n \times \mathcal{Z}^n, \mu^{\otimes n})$. We consider the independent sequence of orthonormal ensembles $\mathcal{F}$ given by $\mathcal{F}_\ell = \setdef{\mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_i(x) \mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_j(y)}{i, j \in \set{0, \ldots, q-1}}$ for any $\ell \in [n]$ (where, recall that $|\mathcal{Z}| = q$). Although as defined $\mathcal{F}_\ell$ has $q^2$ elements, the polynomials we consider will only depend on the subset of characters $\setdef{\mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_{q-1}, \mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_{q-1}}{\ell \in [n]}$. Also, observe that we can choose the characters $\set{\mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_i}$ and $\set{\mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_i}$ such that $\inangle{\mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_i, \mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_j}_\mu = \rho_i \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\set{i=j}}$, where $\rho_1 = \rho(\mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{Z}; \mu)$ is the maximal correlation, and $\rho_i \le \rho$ for all $1 \le i \le q-1$.

Given degree-$d$ multilinear polynomials $A : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$, we consider the polynomial $P : \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z} \to {\mathbb R}^{2k}$ given by $P = (P_1, \ldots, P_{2k})$, where for $j \le k$, we take $P_j({\bm x}, {\bm y}) = A_j({\bm x})$ and for $j > k$, we take $P_j({\bm x}, {\bm y}) = B_{j-k}({\bm y})$. In other words, $P$ is a {\em concatenation} of $A$ and $B$. It is clear that $P$ is also a degree-$d$ multilinear polynomial in $\mathcal{F}$. Also, since $A$ and $B$ are such that $\mathsf{Var}(A_j), \mathsf{Var}(B_j) \le 1$ and $\mathrm{Inf}_\ell(A_j), \mathrm{Inf}_\ell(B_j) \le \tau$ for all $\ell \in [n]$ and $j \in [k]$, we have that for all $j \in [2k]$, it holds that, $\mathsf{Var}(P_j) \le 1$ and $\mathrm{Inf}_\ell(P_j) \le \tau$. Thus, $P$ satisfies all the conditions needed to prove \Cref{lem:invariance}.

We will use the test function $\Psi : {\mathbb R}^{2k} \to {\mathbb R}$, given by $\Psi({\bm u},{\bm v}) := \mathcal{R}_i({\bm u}) \cdot \mathcal{R}_j({\bm v})$, for any given $i, j \in [k]$. It is easy to show that $\mathcal{R}(\cdot)$ is a contraction map (since it is rounding to $\Delta_k$ which is a convex body), and hence any coordinate $\mathcal{R}_i(\cdot)$ has Lipschitz constant of at most $1$. This gives us that our test function $\Psi({\bm u}, {\bm v}) = \mathcal{R}_i({\bm u}) \cdot \mathcal{R}_j({\bm v})$ also has a Lipschitz constant of at most $1$.

We can interpret the invariance principle, as substituting $\setdef{\mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_{q-1}, \mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_{q-1}}{\ell \in [n]}$ by correlated multivariate Gaussians $({\bf g}^{(\ell)}, {\bf h}^{(\ell)}) = (g^{(\ell)}_1, \cdots, g^{(\ell)}_{q-1}, h^{(\ell)}_1, \ldots, h^{(\ell)}_{q-1})$, such that $\mathbb{E} g^{(\ell)}_i h^{(\ell)}_j = \rho_i \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\set{i=j}}$ and $\mathbb{E} g^{(\ell)}_i g^{(\ell)}_j = \mathbb{E} h^{(\ell)}_i h^{(\ell)}_j = \mathbf{1}_{\set{i=j}}$. Thus the invariance principle is taking $P : \mathcal{Z}^n \times \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^{2k}$ and producing $P' : {\mathbb R}^{(q-1)n} \times {\mathbb R}^{(q-1)n} \to {\mathbb R}^{2k}$. Note that the first $k$ coordinates of $P$ are polynomials over the subset $\setdef{\mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_{q-1}}{\ell \in [n]}$ and the latter $k$ coordinates are polynomials over $\setdef{\mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_{q-1}}{\ell \in [n]}$. Hence we can interpret the first $k$ coordinates as $A' : {\mathbb R}^{(q-1)n} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and latter $k$ coordinates as $B' : {\mathbb R}^{(q-1)n} \to {\mathbb R}^k$, and \Cref{lem:invariance} gives us that,
\[ \inabs{\inangle{\mathcal{R}_i(A'), \mathcal{R}_j(B')}_{\mathcal{G}^{\otimes n}} - \inangle{\mathcal{R}_i(A), \mathcal{R}_j(B)}_{\mu^{\otimes n}}} ~\le~ 2^{O(k)} \cdot \inparen{d (8/\sqrt{\alpha})^d \sqrt{\tau}}^{1/3} ~\le~ \delta \]
for a choice of $\tau \le O\inparen{\frac{\delta^{1.5} \cdot \alpha^{d/2}}{2^{O(d)} \cdot 2^{O(k)}}}$.

We are still not done though! We want $\wtilde{A}$ and $\wtilde{B}$ which act on coorrelated inputs sampled from $\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes (q-1)n}$, that is, $({\bf g}^{(\ell)}, {\bf h}^{(\ell)}) = (g^{(\ell)}_1, \cdots, g^{(\ell)}_{q-1}, h^{(\ell)}_1, \ldots, h^{(\ell)}_{q-1})$, such that $\mathbb{E} g^{(\ell)}_i h^{(\ell)}_j = \rho \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\set{i=j}}$ and $\mathbb{E} g^{(\ell)}_i g^{(\ell)}_j = \mathbb{E} h^{(\ell)}_i h^{(\ell)}_j = \mathbf{1}_{\set{i=j}}$. However the correlation pattern obtained in $\mathcal{G}$ is not exactly this. But note that each $\rho_i \le \rho$. Thus, given $(g^{(\ell)}_i, h^{(\ell)}_i)$ with correlation $\rho$, we can simply apply $U_{\rho_i/\rho}$ operator on $h^{(\ell)}_i$ to bring down the correlation from $\rho$ to $\rho_i$. Applying this appropriate operation for every $\ell \in [n]$ and $i \in [q]$, we get our desired $\wtilde{A} : {\mathbb R}^{n \cdot (q-1)} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $\wtilde{B} : {\mathbb R}^{n \cdot (q-1)} \to {\mathbb R}^k$.

The reverse part of the theorem follows similarly as well. Here, we get polynomials $A$ and $B$, that depend only on $\set{\mathcal{X}^{(\ell)}_1}$ and $\set{\mathcal{Y}^{(\ell)}_1}$ respectively.

nodes.name: Proof of \Cref{thm:decidability}
nodes.statement: If we were in the YES case of sc Gap-NIS((Z times Z, mu), V, k, varepsilon), then we have that there exists an N and functions A : Z^N to Delta_k and B : Z^N to Delta_k, such that the distribution nu' = (A(bm x), B(bm y))_(bm x, bm y) sim mu^otimes N is such that d_TV(nu', nu) le varepsilon for some nu in V. Using Crefthm:non-int-sim, with parameter varepsilon/3, we get that there exists functions wtildeA : Z^n_0 to Delta_k and wtildeB : Z^n_0 to Delta_k such that the distribution nu'' = (wtildeA(bm x), wtildeB(bm y))_(bm x, bm y) sim mu^otimes n_0 is such that d_TV(nu'', nu') le varepsilon/3. Hence, d_TV(nu'', nu) le 4varepsilon/3 for some nu in V. In the NO case of sc Gap-NIS((Z times Z, mu), V, k, varepsilon), we have that for all N, in particular for N = n_0, and for all functions A : Z^n_0 to Delta_k and B : Z^n_0 to Delta_k it holds that the distribution nu'' = (A(bm x), B(bm y))_(bm x, bm y) sim mu^otimes n_0 satisfies d_TV(nu'', nu) > 2varepsilon for all nu in V. This naturally gives us a brute force algorithm: Analyze all possible functions wtildeA : Z^n_0 to Delta_k and wtildeB : Z^n_0 to Delta_k to check if there exist functions wtildeA and wtildeB with distribution nu'' = (wtildeA(bm x), wtildeB(bm y))_(bm x, bm y) sim mu^otimes n_0 satisfying d_TV(nu'', nu) le 4varepsilon/3 for some nu in V. For purposes of our algorithm we can replace the range Delta_k by any (varepsilon/3)-cover C, that is, a set of discrete points in Delta_k such that any point in Delta_k is within an ell_1 distance of varepsilon/3 from some point in C. Note that we could choose such a C of size at most (1/varepsilon)^wtildeO(k). This ensures that if indeed such a desired wtildeA and wtildeB exist, then we will find functions wtildeA' : Z^n_0 to C and wtildeB' : Z^n_0 to C such that distribution nu''' = (wtildeA'(bm x), wtildeB'(bm y))_(bm x, bm y) sim mu^otimes n_0 satisfying d_TV(nu''', nu) le 5varepsilon/3 < 2varepsilon for some nu in V. In the YES case, we will find such functions, whereas in the NO case, wtildeA' and wtildeB' as above simply don't exist. The number of pair of functions (wtildeA, wtildeB) to brute force over is |C|^O(|Z|^n_0), which gives us an upper bound on the running time as \[expexpexpinparenpolyinparenk, \ frac1varepsilon, \ frac11-rho_0, \ loginparenfrac1alpha\;.\]
